BALLADE OF THE BOURNE. I, What goal remains for pilgrim feet; Now all our gods are banished?" /air, where sea and sunrise meet, Tall portals bathed in gold and red. From either door a carven head • Smiles down on men full drowsilie, 'Mid nivstic forms of wings outspread Between the Gates of Ivorie. Now, if beyond lie town or street I know not, nor hath any said, Though tongues wag fast and winds are fleet: Some say that there men meet the dead, Or filmy phantoms in their stead, .;d some, "it leads to Arcadie." In sooth I know not, yet would tread :3etween the Gates of Ivorie. For surely there sounds music sweet, With fair delights and perfumes shed, And all things broken made complete, And found again things forfeited; All this for him who scorning dread Shall read the wreathen fantasle, And pass, where no base soul bath sped, Between the Gates of Ivorie. ENVOY. Al, Princess! grasp the golden thread, Rise up and follow fearlesslie, By high desire and longing led Between the Gates of Ivorie. ..—Harper's Magazine. Gs Aiwa R. TOMSON.

His Opening hits were all singles, and be did not fare very well against the bowliog of Berry. Crosfield was run oat, after I playing steadily for 18. and then Tinsley (pro) and Wood- bead became associated. A good stand was made, the bowling being knocked about the field. Berry went on vice Tdatram, and later Scott took theplace of Whitworth. The change worked well, Woodbead being soon bowled by ' Scutt after compiling 21. Tinsley was defying all the bowling, and making some good bits when he was joined by Clarke, the score then standing at 96 for four wickets, which was anything but promising for the Boltonians. Clarke opened with a four bit to the boundary, and the bowling was now being so severely punished that Ashworth went on at Scott's end. Another change was resorted to, H short Ashworth having a turn. Whitworth now sent down a good ball to Warburton, who returned it with some force into the bowler'e left hand, where it was held—a feat for which he was loudly applauded. Podmore was the in-coming bats- man, and the score was approaching 200 when Whitworth dismissed him for four. Clarke was still at the wicket, playing as steadily as ever, and knocking the bowling about with ease. Kirkham was the tact batsman, and early on ought to have been run out. Clarke was at length bowled by Tristram, and the innings closed for 213. Clarke had ob- tained 72, including a grand leg hit out of the ground. Bol- ton began with Berry and Grey. There was a larger crowd outside the inn at Bally- goyle than one would have thought could have been gathered from such a scantily populated district, but given anything of intense interest and the very earth seems to grow people. Through the midst of them alone and unguarded, Vincent 'Lorraine rode up to-the door, and only smiled as he heard the groans that greeted his appearance. The smiled deepened when he caught sight of a beau- tiful face on the outskirts of the throng, and he bent low, lifting his hit. lie had ,half hoped to see her to-day; but he-noted that only Terence O'Conor rode, with her. Traty was not by her side. The sympathies of the jury were with Patrick Doolan but their duty was too clean cut for even an Irish jury to evade; and besides, they were more impressed than they weuld have owned by the haughty and perfectly cool mien of the very handsome and aristocratic lord of Curramore ; and the Irish, it must be remembered, are peculiarly sensitive to the influence of personnel. It was impossible to suggest that -Lorraine bad antici- pated the shot, and equally impossible to blame amen for defending his own life • but the coroner remarked that he thought Misther Lorraine might have taken the throuble to see if the poor bhoy still lived. "He had better measure than he deserved„' was Lorraine's reply to this; "for if he had been living he would have only merited another bullet to put an end to him; and that I would have spared him, but .I fancy he would not have dealt so by me.'

Which could not be well gainsaid. The verdict was a foregone conclusion—that Patrick Doolani' met his death by a pistol shot, and that such pistol shot was fired in self-defence; hut the jury added a rider ex- pressing a hdpb that ?Misther Lorraine would deal kindly by to poor widow, and allow her to kape the ' howld ing." "Whether she can pay the rent ahrcultivate the land or nq ?" observed Lorraine, laughing. "I have been in many lands and among many people, gentle- men, but I never—even in California—met with such barbarous ideas of rights and contracts as exist 4n this land of Erin. Good morning." And Lorraine bowed and turned to quit the room, leaving coroner, jury, and crowd " spacheless " with amazement and indignation. Clearly, Misther Lorraine was a problem not easy of solution—a "land question" in himself. , He mounted his horse, and the crowd fell back, glowering at him as he rode among them, and reached the spot where HYacinth'and Terence had halted. 'So you are not committed for murder?" said O'Conor, as Lorraine shook hands with Hyacinth. "No ; but they all think it murder. The jury hoped I would leave Mrs: Doolan in the holding, which is a little cool, I think." They wheeled their horses and rode away, the crowd sending a few shouts and groans after them. Most of the conversation was carried on between Terence and Lorraine; Hyacinth said but little, answering Lorraine when he spoke to her as briefly as possible. When they reached the point where the Englishman turned off to Curramore, Terence: said gravely— "Mr. Lorraine, 'tis not much use warning- you; but I hope you will take this one—not to sit within range in the line of any window." "Thanks. • I think I must rig them up a dummy as a trap.. So if you hear of my being shot through the window, wait a little before you conclude it is all over with me. ...in revair."

He said no more than those two words to Hyacinth when she gave him her hand; but she felt, though Terence could not see, how tightly his hand closed over hers, giving a significance that Hyacinth resented to the mellifluous "Au revoir," though it was not all resentment that made her heart beat so, and her hand seem to retain so long the sense of that masterful clasp. When Terence spoke of Lorraine she answered carelessly, changed the subject, and proposed a gallop. Terence could make nothing of her. That night—at twelve o'clock—a man, masked with crape, prowled under the walls of Curranaore Castle, glancing up at the windows. "He sits up till one and • two av a marning," he muttered ; "pretty hours .to kape ; but them's his profligit ways, and divil a bit I'd wish them althered jist now. The libery's in the little tower, and bike enough hell be there—there was a bight in it siveral.toimes lately. Ah !" He drew a quick breath, and halted. Among the black, frowning group of buildings a single square of light appeared, and against the light was a motionless, indefinite shadow, which, as far as Dermot Grady's gleaming eyes could make out, appeared to be the figure of a man seated at a table, his back towards the window, which was veiled by a blind or curtain. One• moment the man stood still gazing. All was silent around. Not a breath stirred over the dreary waste; nature herself seemed to favour the black deed the man had come there to work, for the night was obscure, not even a star shone in the clouded heavens. Grady set his teeth, and slowly lifted his rifle to his shoulder. "Ye're done for this toime, Misther Lorraine," he whispered.' "Ye can go to the divil an' tell him Dermot Grady sint ye there !" He took deliberate aim, and fired. Crash went the bullet through the glass, and in the same second the shadow disappeared and the light also vanished. Had Lorraine fallen? Grady turned and fled; but as he fled he heard a pistol shot, and a bullet whizzed close past him. With an awful oath the man halted. He had missed Lorraine !—missed him though he had fired straight at him. The villain wiped the drops from his brow. By what mysterious agency was the hated Sassenach protected? Nothing but a supernatural power could have saved him to-night! It was some- thing more than physical fear that made Grady rnsh on, casting many a fearful glance'behind hkm: Vincent Lorraine was something more than a man. He (Grady) would make no more attempts to shoot him; but held have the spalpeen's blood yet, aye, if he was the divil himself, as he half believed he was. And Vincent Lorraine threw down his pistol and laughed, a merry reckless laugh. His rum had succeeded admirably; a coat and cap on the back of a tall-backed chair had played a more important part than usually falls to the lot of inanimate objects. "The villain deserves the coat," said Lorraine, presently striking a light," "only it wouldn't fit him; —he has made a hole clean through it. If that had been you, Mr. Vincent Bertram Lorraine, you would have taken a swift flight--somewhere. And I won- der,"—he added this after a pause, and his brow darkened—" I wonder how much Hyacinth would care? Your own lips must tell me that, NM amour; and I will take no nay from them. What made her treat me as she did to-day? Trifling? No; it would be in a London or Paris belle, but not in this sweet shamrock. She thinks I am trifling—thinks me a row& profligate —what you will that is evil, and—well : young Mans- ..field was right; lam not worthy to touch her hand; and yet I must touch it, hold it, claim it, draw her to my heart, enfold her in my life. She is part of my life now. I cannot stab one half my heart to death and leave tlae other half living; and no more can I root out this flower. It must be—it`shall be all my own."

The next day was a Saint's day, and it was after Miu3S That Hyacinth first heard the news of the attempt of the previous night on Vincent' Lorraine's life, and its failure. Hyacinth kept her own counsel, but felt inclined to laugh, for she guessed at once how it was that the murderer "missed "his mark.
"That was Dermot Grady who fired that shot, know," said the girl, as she and her mother walked homewards, "and Lorraine will suspect him; but he will serve the notice on him all the same."

A correct surmise; for at two o'clock that day Vincent Lorraine rode up to Grady's farm, and, with- out dismounting, presented the farmer with his notice to quit. The unparalleled daring of the man fairly appalled the peasantry; they puld hardly believe their " sinses "; Lorraine must in some way bear a charmed life, or he could never adventure it as he did. And meanwhile a' heavy shadow had fallen on the Wood Cottage. Mrs. Desmond had hardly commented on Hyacinth's refusal of her cousin's suit; and would —under ordinary circumstances— have been beat pleased that she should give her hand to a man whose.

nature was more in harmony with her own; but now Mrs. Desmond was more than half inclined to regret her daughter's decision. She dreaded Vincent Lorraine;. she believed him to be a thohmighly unscrupulous man, and though she had no distinct idea of what he might do, or even whether he wished to make Hyacinth his wife, she still felt nervous, and heartily wished him anywhere but at Curramore. She :Aa'!,a nothing to Hyacinth of these fears, and 40%7g-flee& less, for she soon perceived that the giTtlropped her long rides and rambles, though it-e- still went among the cottages of the pouttmtry—though less, as Mrs. Desmond believetlyimong Lorraine's tenants than &C lad been us'a to do. In this impression, however, she was mistaken; Hyacinth simply practised mental reservation, and Mrs. Desmond not unnaturally jumped at the conclusion, that evidently wishing to avoid the lord of Curramore, the girl was not ,so likely to go among his tenants. But Hyacinth hid' a motive which she kept to herself. She knew the cha- racter_gf oWn'People, and of 'some of these farmers in 'particular, far too, well to supposefor a moment that they intended to give up all attempts on the life .of their detested landlord. They were afraid to fire from behind a hedge; no man cared to run so deadly a risk; but that only meant that they would. bide their time the While they conmeted some more certain means of accomplishing their fell purpose.; and Hyacinth deter- milled that murder should not be done if she could pre- vent it.. Of .coutse the people were guarded in her presence. She had, over and over again fearlessly, denounced their views itna. practices; but the girl. posdessed in a pre-eminent degree the quickness of eye and ear characteristic of her country; anti with these'' faculties she combined a capacity rare in the young— of keeping her thoughts concealed while her face would give no idea of' hiding anything. She. could laugh and talk With one person while really, giving her attention to another; and thus would notice many a look or gesture; hearken to ..many a tone or intlecticm which even a very keen observer would have supposed had made no impression on her senses. . Days passed on, and nothing unusual occurred. Ballygoyle. Regan, refusing to pay his rent, had received notice to quit, and both: her and Grady de- clared that they didn't mean to quit. On the: pther hand, Dan Murphy had called on Mrs. Doolan and told, her that Mr. Lorraine would forgive the arrears' of) rent, and allow her to keep on the farm at a melt. loiver r6ntal, for another year at least. This genetiMil act clearly showed that Lorraine was not vindictive,. and was too just and too proud to fear, showing mercy where mercy was due, lost it should be misinterpreted: He gained small thanks from the peasants for his,for;- bearance to the widow of Isis would-be murderer; but he gained what—if he bad known of it—she would have valued more than the acclamations of a nation--.Byti- cinth Desmond's approbation. Days passed, and Hyacinth did, not meet Vincent, Lorraine. She saw him onse in' the distance, and urging Shemus forward, rode quickly away; and she 'could not be sure whether he had seen her or not; but when, after five days, she still did not meet him, she began to think that she had needlessly abandoned her long rambles, for that already Los ra no was tiring of the pastime, and did not care to seek her; or wished to break off an intercourse which could not go much further without pledging him to more than-he intended to fulfil. "I wish he would go away altogether," she said to herself. "I was happy enough till be came, and now everything seems dismal." ' Such words as this she was saying to herself one afternoon as she Ivalked towards Grady's farm; she wanted to see Biddy, who was getting much better, and as she walked she glanced about her, but saw no sign of the lord of Curramore; and there was no great, likelihood of meeting ,him 'in any of his tenants' houses I , • . The sun had nearly set when she started homewards, taking ti short cut that lay across some fields—a path little trodden, and out of sight of any house, but Hyacinth had no cause to fear anyone; neither man nor woman in Ballygoylp wonld have lifted a hand to harm Mias Hyacinth; besides which, country-bred girls have not the horror of solitudes that distinguishes their town sisters. • She walked on quickly, swinging her hat and singing to herself, though not in quite the old blithesome way, and had just reached the stile that separated the meadow land from the long stretch of moorland called the Common, when she heard a sound behind her that made her heart leap up and the crimson rush in a flood to her face, to fade the next moment ,into perfect whiteness. The swift measured stroke of a horse's hoofs. The rider might have been Terence, for if he had seen her he would have followed her, though this was not a usual horse road; but the girl's true instinct told her it was not Terence. She stopped and turned :round., She could not avoid Lorraine now, ant), perhaps. , although he must have followed her, through the fields, it was mere chance his having seen her. Yes, there he was, riding at a quick eot, and as the girl turned, he . raised his hat and bowed; the next moment he had flung him- self from his horse and stood before her. Shp gave him her hand frankly then; there was nothing else to be done. He took it in his own, and bent his bead a's if he would have kissed it, but seemed to change his mind, and only kept it in his close strong clasp as he said, half jestingly-r— -" I must crave your grace, although it is all. un- wittingly that I deprived you of your long rides and walks. Did you think I did not know you avoided use ?"

--The girl flushed crimson, but gave him ohe quick, haughty look, drawing her hand from his, as she answered— " You might have known it—you were to blame-- not I." " Yes, I was to blame," said Lorraine, quietly, " and sans doute, when days passed and you did not see me, , you thought I was tired of amusing myself—your look answers me; but there you were mistaken—pardon— and I only practised that strategy which is permissible, I think, in all such circumstances. I kept away—l did not: seek to meet you; you began to feel secure, and— have I not been successful ?" "Up to this point, yes," the girl answered, in that same manner, "but lam tired of amusement, if you are not. So, good evening ! " She laid her hand on the stile, close to which she stood, as if to cross it; but Lorraine stepped forwards, and as, instinctively, she drew back, he placed himself between her and the step of the stile. "Forgive me," he said, coolly, "but I have not waited five days to see you, to be dismissed, when at last suc- cess crowned my patience, with a few scornful words. - Do you in your heart believe, Hyacinth, that all this time I have been simply trifling?" Hyacinth had turned very white, and started at the bold utterance of her Christian name; but she did not lift her eyes, nor—though Lorraine paused for a reply —was one forthcoming. He went on, with a slight, but subtle change of tone and manner that the girl felt at once. "I think you must know that only two meetings be- tween you and me were accidental. I don't know whether I loved you the first time I saw you—one can- not analyse such impressions; but I saw that day the only woman of whom I ever said, 'Her life and mine are one,' and I sought, and easily found, opportunities of meeting you again. And you believed—believe now —that I only wanted to while away the tedious hours of a country life, and that I had at last grown weary of the amusement,' or, perchance—having some rag of honour left,—did not care to go too far, having no thought beyond 'amusement '—" "Stay!" Hyacinth burst out abruptly, putting out her hand as if to veil the blinding light cast on her in- nermost thoughts—struck with an agonised fear that she had misjudged the man, that, roué though he was, he really loved her. "Stay, I must not hear you—if I have wronged you, forgive me. How should I think you cared for me more than you have cared for many others? lam but a wild country girl—scarcely more than a child—you have all the world can give, and you have the world to choose from." "I have nothing," said Lorraine, passionately, "if I have not you. Not hear me Nay, but you must hear me! I ask no mercy—no immunity for the past. God knows my life has been evil enough to one so pure as you, but I call Him to witness that from the moment I saw you my every thought has been yours; aye, and shall be yours in life and in death. Do you think that , love means to me only a passing passion, leaving scarcely a memory behind it? I tell you I, roue, profli- gate—call me these and worse if you will—never knew what love was till I met you. Is ,it one more sin added to the iong account to ask you to yield your spotless life to my keeping, to yield your hand to my clasp, un- worthy to enfold it? I care not. I love you; give the your love, and so blot out the past; the future I give to you." With breath that rose and fell in heavy throbs, with hands tightly clenched, and wild, troubled eyes that dared not face the man who spoke, Hyacinth heard ;those passionate words that half pleaded for love, half claimed possession; but to the noble nature appealed to, the plea, "I love you; I give the future to you," was all but irresistible. The very disdain of all other plea, the pride, the chivalrous sense of truth which not only forbade all subterfuge, but owned unworthiness with what might seem almost cynical frankness, struck, to Hyacinth's fine and subtle sense, the keynote of a grand nobility of soul. It is not often, perhaps, that a lover owns to the woman whose favour he seeks that he has justly earned the name of roué, and is doing a , 'daring thing to ask her to overlook an evil past; but eveuVW.l.....M

Sir War. HART Drxe-, in moving the second read- ing of the Technical Instruction Bill, said the primary object of the measure was tp enlarge the powers of the Science and Art Department, so as to en- able technical 'instruction of a primary charactei to be supplied 'to echolars who have passed the sixth standard. It "was proposed in this way to allow such scholars to mn.dergo two or three yeare' training; not for the purpose,ef teaching them a trade, but in order that they might receive that kind of training of the eye and band in wood and ironwork and other matters that would be .of the greatest service to them on entering into workeitops and other places in which trades were carried en. He 'denied that there-was any foundation for the objection that the bill would 'have the effect of largely increasing the rates. It was proposed that classes should be established in existing buildings, where a vast amount of training could be afforded. Neither was therenny ground for the fear that expensive schools of a secondary character would 'be get up under 'the measure. He had found that ',as regarded the metropOlis it would be impoislble to apply the third clause of the' bill to London, and afterconsulting the , .metropolitan members he proposed to add to Clause 2 a provision that the local authorities should incur no ex- pense under the bill without consulting the ratepayers. This provision it was not intended tmeictend to all dis- tricts ender the bill. He regrettell thatthe measure did not =propose' to afford practical training in agriculture; and as tdthe expense that would' be incurred, the main partion,df' that would be the payment of the teachers, more =than` four-fifths of whose' emkuments would be ,paia .by the fees of the scholars, sothat the remaining portion of the cost would he hut a• very slight burden on the 'ratepayers. Mr. 'STANLEY LEIGHTON regarded the measure as one 'that would add materially 'to' themes, and moved, as an amendment, that, while the' House was desirous of seeing increased facilities for 'technical instruction .85i:reeled it was not prepared to proceed with a' Measure which imposed a new charge on thematepayers for that, purpose until such changes had been made in the inci- , dence of local taxation as will secure the equitable con- tribution of all classes of the commuility to the rates. 'Colonel' ETRE seconded the amendment, urging that the effect of the bill would be to throw an additional tax ens the' land, and that, as its object was to confer a national benefit, the cost ought to be charged .= the consolidated , fund. . _

The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER pointed out that the'bill would be purely voluntarY,in its operation, and would have very little application,to the rural districts. 'Consequently as it would mainly Abe adopted by the towns,and would be carried out by means supplied by the urban ratepayers, the agricultural community would not .be 'called upon for any contribution toward the 'charges that mig It arise under it. 'lf, however, as had been contended, the charge was thrown upon the Con- solidated Fund, the agricultural interest, which con- tributed largely to the national esehequer would in that case be called upon to pay a large proportion of the cost. Thelpill was deemed by the Government to be urgently needed, and it was only just that the people of the towns in which it would operate, and who would be specially advantaged by its adoption should' defray the charge. The estimate of the Science and Art Elf pwtment was that for the first three years the number • who would be likely to receive technical training • under the measure would' be• about 12,000. •

Sir!it'Txmrt.n stipported the measure. Mr.lfumpau,s, though glad to welcome any measure 'from :any party that would advance in any way the cause of 'education, nevertheless looked upon some por- tione,of the present measure with repugnance, and was espeCially.anxious to see the provincial towns placed on an • -equal footing of equality With the metropolis. The right hon. gentleman cited the example set by Germany in the promotion of technical education, as one that England would do well to follow, and strongly deprecated the parsimonious views that had been ex- pressed. by hon. gentlemen who had ,opposed the bill. He denied that there .was any danger .to the voluntary schools .in what was proposed by thabill. Mr. 'W. H. SMITE( said the Government had satisfied themselves that it was absolutely impossible that the bill could impose any additional burthen on the agricul- tural ,community, and lie was convinced it would be unwiseanti impolitic for agricultural members to place any obstaele in the way of urban communities availing themselves of the advantages of the bill. They therefore , appealed to. them to withdraw their opposition to the second reading of the bill. _ Mr. 15.'82.mm protested against the very narrow and disappointing scope of the bill. Mr. Lnas.said that until the last member rose it seemed as if there was not a Tory member who was not an agri- cultural member. As a Conservative member of an urban constituency, he supported. the bill. Mr. STANDBY LEIGHTON declined to withdraw his amendment, .and At was negatived without a divisian amid cheers. - -

div.p: TIIE I,,XAMINER. SATURDAY, A UGUSI 13, 1887.
CURRENT POLITICS.
The Peen Mall Gazette has published the text of Mr. O'Donnell's statement of his case against The Times. He claims £50,000 damages.

Sir Henry James, speaking at a Unionist county de- monstration on Saturday, at Hereford, said the Liberal Unionists were being condemned for keeping improper company; but, though not hard-hearted, they wanted to know why, if they were right in opposing ?dr. Glad- stone's Home Rule schome last year, they were wrong in continuing that attitude. They studied in vain Mr. Gladstone's every word in the hope of finding reason to suppose that the policy he propounded had been aban- doned. .

Mr. John Bright has signed the memorial to the President and the Congress of the United States in favour of the establishment of a court of international arbitration for the settlement of disputes that may arise between England and America. One hundred and seventy-three English, Welsh, and Scotch members of the House of Commons have attached their signatures to the memorial, and nine members have signified their intention of joining the deputation which will proceed to America in the autumn for the purpose of presenting it. Sir Chas. Russell, speaking at Chatham on Monday afternoon, after laying the foundation-stone of a new Liberal club, said when the Liberal Government pro- ceeded to deal with the Irish question they found two opposing powers to reconcile—one the Government of the Queen, backed by thirty thousand soldiers, besides the bayonets of constables; and the other an unconsti- tutional, but nevertheless great, power, because it was supported by a majority of the Irish people. Mr. Glad- stone's policy was to consolidate these two forces, and to put upon the Nationalist leaders the responsibility of their teaching. Mr. Gladstone arrived at Chester Station at 9 33 on Saturday night, having travelled by the 5 30 express from Euston. The right hon. gentleman—who, with Mrs. Gladstone, occupied a special saloon carriage—was heartily cheered by a large crowd on the platform. Cheers were given for "The Grand Old Man," for " Mr. Brunner," and for " Northwich," and one person called out, "We will send you another helper from Northwich," This elicited from Mr. Gladstone the remark, "1 hope you will." Mr. Gladstone cordially shook hands with the Rev. Father M‘Enerv, of Wicklow, who explained that he presided at the Irish Convention held at Wick- low, at which Mr. Parnell laid down his policy with regard to the coming elections. Mr. Gladstone, in the course of a short conversation with the reverend father, observed that the Irish priesthood now had a great work to perform in common with the people. By the courtesy of the London and North-Western Railway Officials, a special engine was attached to the saloon carriage, and it was taken to 'Sandycroft Station, whence Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone ,drove to Haward en. _

MR. erLiDSTORR ON " COERCION WITIIOI7T CRIME."—Mr. Gladstone has written as follows to Mr. T. A. Fore, Shel- bourne Hotel, Dublin:—" Hawarden Castle, August 10.— Dear sir,—The evidence which you have supplied in your tract, 4 Coercion Without Crime,' from the charges of judges reporting on matters of fact within their judicial cognis- ance, appears to illustrate vividly the freedom of Ireland from crime, and unless it can be effectually answered, to Illustrate -strongly the absurdity as well as the cruelty of the measure which was directed by the Legislature against combination under the name of crime, and which is now at by-elections coming under review by a portion of the con- stituencies of the country—Your faithful servant, W. E. 41L4DSTONE."

FOREST FIRES ;IN AMERICA.—DESTRUCTION OF A TOWN. NEW YOD2I,'WEDNESDAY.—Forest fires are doing great damage in ,parts of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Indiana, especially in the farming districts. Sandusky, the csunty town of Simile° conntv, Michigan, has been destroyed by fire. PRINCE FERDINAND'S JOURNEY TO • BULGARIA.

VIENNA, 3 HVESDAY.—Prince Ferdinand of Coburg ar- rived at Orsova at midnight last night, and remained there till this morninz, when he resumed the journey at five o'clock. The Prince will probably take the oath before the Bohranje at Tirnova on Tuesday next. He will then issue a manifesto to the Bulgarian nation, and the Regency and the Ministry will resign. It is believed that the Regent Sternbuloff will be the new President of the Ministry.

GERMANY. thurrang, SATURDAY.—The Emperor Francis Joseph arriveli here at two o'clock this afternoon, and met with an enthusiastic reception from the inhabitants and visitors. His Majesty proceeded to Badesehloss, the Emperor William's residence. The meeting between the Monarchs was marked by great warmth on both sides. ROME, MONDAY NlGHT.—Yesterday the Tope sent a letter to the Emperor of Germany at Gastein, thanking him for his recent gift. 'The letter is most cordial in tone. It alludes to the prominent part taken personally'by his Majesty in re-establishing religious peace, and in con- dusien says that the accord between the Pope and the Emperor will also contribute to certain peace in Europe. MT. PETERSBURG MONDAY NIGHT.—M. Katkoff's death and 'funeral and the political manifestations in connec- tion therewith have for some days absorbed the Russian public, and political occurrences abroad have been quite neglected. To•day, however, the Liberal -victory at Glasgow is much commented upon inull political circles here. The opinion appears at present that the Home Rule party is making remarkably rapid progress. Opinion here is convinced that if there were a dissolu- tion at the present moment there would be a large majority for Mr. Gladstone. PARIS, MONDAY.—A decree of the Prefect of the depart- ment of Meurthe and Moselle allows the German firm of VVeisbach, of Embermenil, three monthS' grace before closing their toy manufactory. It is understood this extension of time had been conceded in order to give the firm the opportunity to dispose a their -stock of goods. The Liberti affirms that the closing of the factory has not led to any diplomatic representations. A ,telegram from Paris says that Baron Billing, late French Ambassador to Sweden, has been .expelled from Alsace, where he was visiting some friends. FRANOE.—THE BOUL A. N E'R -FERRY PIASOO.—A DUELLIST PUNISHED.

PARIS, SATURDAY.—A duel took place to-day between M. Reinach, director of the Republuine Francaise, and‘M. Magnier, director of the Evenonent, the cause being a dis- pute-respecting the Boulanger-Ferry affair. M.'Reinach was wounded in the chest.

Pests, SATURDAY.—M. Ferry's seconds having taken no further steps yesterday with a view to arrange the conditions of an encounter between the ex-Premier and General Boulanger, the incident now appears to'be defi- nitely closed. PARTS, MONDAY—General Boulanger has ;just ad- dressed the following letters to General Faverot and Comte Dillon, the two gentlemen who acted as his seconds in the affair with M. Jules Ferry have just received the letter from M. Ferry to his seconds. That letter suggests to me but one reflection. Having 'been insulted by M. Ferry I wished to fight a serious duel and not one attended by scarcely any danger. Public opinion will jutlge between one who, at a long distance off, insults a general and will grant him only a derisory reparation, and myself, who purposed to risk my life to avenge my honour ,as a soldier. A cordial shake of the hands to you." 'ANOTHER. ALPINE DISASTER.

BERNE, STURDY.— A dispatch just to band from Zermatt states that another serious disaster has eccurred there. 'Doctors Lammer and Lorria, both members of the Vienna Alpine Club, decided to ascend be Matter- horn without guides. They had got about half-way up when they lost their way, and fell over 4 precipice. As they did, not return to their hotel at 7,ermatt, it was feared that they had met with some mishap. A search party was organised in the village, and succeeded in finding the unfortunate climbers. Both were still living, but theythad sustained such terrible injuries that their recovery is doubtful. They are being well cared for at Zermatt, FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTAN.

SIMLA, SATURDAY.—Cvnflicting accounts continue to be received, concerning the fighting alleged to have °marred on • the 28th ult. between the Afghan troops under Gholana Hyder Khan and the Ghilzals, beyond Hotel Dab& The Ameer's General reports having gained the victory,and inflicted great slaughter on the enemy, whereas, according to news • received from Cabul, the Ghilzais woroviotorious.

div.head: NATIONAL EISTEDDFOD OF WALES. •
div.p: THE NATIONAL EISTEDDFOD OF WALES. •

'The National, Eisteddfod of Wales opened on Tuesday at the Royal Albert Hall, London, under the presi- dency of Lord Mostyn, who was received with the cus- tomary ceremonies. After poetical addresses by some of the principaltards, the President delivered an address, and various choral competitions followed. Previous to the Eisteddfod meeting, the Ancient Hardie Gorsedd was held in the open ai ir n Hyde Park, in the presence of thousands of spectators. The following letter from Mr. Gladstone, addressed to Mr. El. Richard, MP., on August 4th, was read : tt After addressing the representative London meet- ing, last Friday, I caught from exposure a sore throat, which passed to a slight cough, and I was con- fined to bed until yesterday. It has way but could not undertake so soon after the ULS. to address .a public meeting on the 9th. It is true that I had in- tended, and still intend, to go to Hawarden this week, but even if in London, I should not have been able to undertake the office of President of the Eisteddfod. I am not quite sure in what relation the in- tended Metropolitan meeting stands to the com- ing ,Eisteddfod of North Wales ; but I do not the less heartily on that account wish entire sucess,to both. The exertions of devoted Welshmen in the front rank, of whom you personally stand, have taughttas to comprehend how,much reason Wales has to look carefully to the custody, and to enlarge the know- ledge of the stores of treasure with which her own history and literature have provided her. It ap- pears to methat the gen.v4 become more and more aware as time proceeds h.- • fully justified, and bow much required, are these commemorative celebra- tions. There are, indeed, some who think that :ill local distinctions ought, to be melted down 4nto a level of uni- formity; but if the formation of individual characters, each upon their own type, is ft great providential pur- pose of our existence on earth, it is surely wise to cherish and develop everything that has an educating power; and among such instruments it is, I suppose, indisputable that the traditions of language, literature, and history usually held a most important place. The devoted patriotism of the natives of the Principality of Welshmen will, I am cimfident, only make them better subjects and better Britons. Accept, therefore, my cor- dial good wishes ior the celebration." The PRESIDENT, in his opening address, referred to the history of Eisteddfodau, and justified their existence on the ground that they encouraged the development of national literature and music. The evening was devoted to a concert of Welsh airs land melodies, rendered by the Eisteddfod Choir and by I professional soloists, amongst whom were Madame Edith Wynne, Miss Mary Davies, Miss Ele:rupr Rees, Mr, Lucas Williams, and Mr. James Sauvage. Mr. John Tommas, Parpigl f.to her Majesty, pre a harp solo.

The Whitby Moots have been bti fire owiag to the ex,, cessive heat. •

Salim Faris Effendi, a Turkish author, rtowin London, as written, with a view to publication, a work on the decadence of England in the East. , I On Saturday, John Bacon, a quarryman, whilst felling a tree at the top of a quarry near Haddon Hall, Derby- shire, fell a distance of 63 feet, and was instantly II By a spark freq.' a passing train a serious fire was caused on Monday on tile estate of the Speaker of the ' House of Commons at Sandy, Bedfordshire. Ten acres :of trees and n'orse were destroyed, with much game:

CAPITAL PNCE BEherrFn.—The Governor Of War.. wick Gaol has received a telegram from the Home Office ;trespiting, daring her M .jestrta pleasure, the sentence lad death nassed upon Fanny Goldby at the recent War- Iwick Assizes for the murder of her illegitimate child' at Leek Wootton. t The electric light is being tried in the Scotch fisheries. ''.411.8 fish are invariably attracted by a strong light, a Asowerftil electric-lighting apparatus has been fitted to a ateainer plying on the fishing grounds round the Isle of 'May, at the mouth of the Firth of Forth. It is expected' that the brilliant lure wit bring a good haul. I EXTRAORDINARY VEREIOT AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.—itt 'the 'Liverpool Assizes on'Moriday, David Lewis, a collier, 'of lace-in-Makerfield, was indicted for brutallY assault- ' inglis wife. Evidence was given of the prisoner biting .and striking the woman, who is still under medical Care. The jury, to the astonishment of the court, returned a !verdict of not guilty. The clerk was so surprised that he twice repeated the question, and the judge, in dis- -dharging the prisoner, said that, any other jury would have convicted him. Such a verdict, was an encourage- ment to drunken men to ill-treat their wives. TUE QUEEN AND THE IMPERIAL INSTITUTE : A STRANGE :STORY.—Some time ago a Ladies' 'Committee in Govan 'raised money to.endow in honour of the Queen's Jubilee, i beds n the Dunoon Convalescent Home. They asked the Queen to allow the beds to be called "Victoria beds." Captain M'Lean,.at a meeting of the Govan Police Com- missioners onMortday; asked whether it VMS true that the Queen had refused her sanction. Mr. James Kirkwood said Mrs. Bird, secretary to the ladies' Committee, had received &letter from 'Sir Henry Ponsonby expressing the Queents'disapproval at the'money not being sent to the ImmitilllnStitute Fund, and stating that the Queen under the Circumstances declined to express an opinion. Dam 7N 'AN HOSPITAL OF AN HEIR TO A PEERAGE.- Viscouvrt Forth, the grandson and heir to the title of the Earl of Perth and Melfort, who emigrated to the States a few years .ago in consequence of having contracted a tmesaltianre, died on Thursday, leaving one daughter, aged eight years, and a widow. They had lived in re- spectablnpoverty upon his earnings in humble capacities untilthe viscount's broken health left them dependent upon her needle and upon charity. The remittances from 'England were scanty and uncertain, although lat- terly urgent appeals had been sent for help. The de- ceased was' born in 1856, and was the only son of Lord Perth's second son. Lord Perth is in his fist year, and has .one daughter living, and this little great grand- daughter in'New York.

A ' DISPIITID BEQUEST TO MR. BRADLAUGH.—An appeal of Mr. Bradlaugh, M. P.,'and Mr. G. Payne, of Manchester. against an order of the Vice-Chancellor of the County Palatine Omit came up for judgment ori Friday before ' the 'Lords Uustices. The Vice-Chancellor had admitted .mttain evidence which the appellants considered ought +dot to have been received in the hearing of an action in , connection with the will of Mr. Jonas Spencer, of Oti 1 Trafford, Who had left £5OO to the appellants to apply to purposes communicated to them secretly by the testator, land the mat of the estate was given to trustees. Action 'was taken in the Palatine Court, where evidence was ,accepted to show that the gift was one of trust, and it was the right to put in this evidence that was contested. The Lords Justices held that the evidence in question •was properly received, and that the appeal failed. 'BRUTAL MURDER OF A POLICEMAN BY POACHERS.— The body et a police constable named William Brown was fortrid in the canal at Pendeford, near Wolver- hampton, on Sunday morning, in circumstances widen leave little room for doubt that the man had been thrown into the water by fish poachers in the course of the night. t•Two.men who were drinking at a beerhouse at which Brown called late on Saturday night, near the scene ef l the murder, are suspected, but the police are unable to I trace their movements after they left the house. Neither can either of them be found. It is supposed the officer 'followed the men down to the fishing preserve close to the canal, where his body was found, and that whilst attempting their arrest, he was overpowered and killed.

WIFE MoanEris.—An old man named Stephen Mackay., employed as a gardener, was apprehended at Dundee on Saturday on the charge of murdering his wife. The parties, who had been drinking, quarrelled in the morn- ing, and in the heat of the dispute Mackay, it is alleged, lifted an iron poker, and struck his wife a severe blow with it. Her skull was fractured, and she died a few hours after being removed to the hospital.—At an in- quest held at the village of Middle, near Shrewsbury, on the body of the wife of Charles Kynaston, farmer, the jury returned a verdict of "Wilful murder" against the husband. Me pair frequently quarrelled, and on Mon- day week, deceased, who occupied a separate room, was found dead. A gun was lying on the bed, and there was a shot in the deceased's mouth. It was elicited that Kynaston was the reputed father of the child of one of his servants. CLOSING OF THE LEEDS AND LIVERPOOL CANAL AT BINGLEY.—The bargemen passing through Apperley and Rodley to Leeds, on Sunday, reported that in consequence of the continued drought the Leeds and Liverpool Canal was closed as far down as Binglev on Saturday evening against traffic. The water was drained off through the locks into the lower reaches, in order that communica- tion may be kept open as long as possible between Leeds and the various wharves along the route up to Bingley. Notwithstanding the fact that much lighter loads have been carried during the past week or two, traffic has been greatly impeded in consequence of the shallow dept of water in the cut, and on Sunday, although the water was a little higher through the quantity let in from the upper reaches, empty barges, when not kept in mid- 4ream, grated on the bottom of the cut. MURDEROUS ASSAULT.—On Saturday afternoon a man named Beasley, who reside:3 in Hulme, went to the resi- dence of his sister, Mrs. Ludlam, the wife of a butcher carrying on business at Withington, and after asking for a knife wherewith to cut his thniat, proceeded to strike his sister with a shovel. This was taken from him by a shopman named Bowker, whom he afterwards endea- voured to hit with a cleaver. Being prevented from doing this, he turned upon an elderly gentleman named named Brooks, and struck him such a violent blow on the side of the head that it is reported to have caused a fracture of the skull. Beasley, who is said to have oc- casionally acted strangely since he met with an accident about two years ago which injured his spine, was after- wards taken into custody.—At Manchester, on Monday, Beasley was charged with attempted murder. The old gentleman, Brooks, is not likely to recover. The prisoner was remsnded for medical inquiries.

BATHING FATALITIES.—The clothes of Mr. J. Wooton, professor of music, Walsall, were on Saturday found on the margin of the Park Lime Pit Pools, Rushall, a deep expanse of water communicating with very old limestone workings. It is assumed that Mr. Wooton went bathing in the poOI and was drowned.—On Saturday Matthew Cunningham. puddler, employed at Bowling Foundry, was drowned while bathing in the reservoir at the works. —Thomas Evans, boatman, Egrernont, reported to the New Brighton police, on Sunday, that at 330 that morn- ing he VMS proceeding in his boat down the Rock Channel when lie saw a gig containing four persons capsize. He wasabout half a mile away from the scene of the acci- dent, and immediately went to the assistance of the .struggling men. He succeeded in saving three men, but a fourth was drowned. The wind was blowing hard at the time, and the 'boat was struck by a sudden squall. The man drowned was John Cook. Liverpool.--A young man named Alfred Heap, 18 years of ageLiscard, was bathing in the Mersey on Sunday morning, near the Magazines, New Brighton, when he was drowned.

MeatNo Lova To A Monran-tx-LAw.—Florna LE TRAGEDY.—A shocking crime is reported from Valetta, near Toulon. A grocer named Anicet lost his young wife about four months ago. Latterly he became violently enamoured of his mother-in-law, a Mdme. Frebois, aged 48 years, in whose house he was living. The widow thought at first that her son-in-law was mailbag game of her, but as he renewed his extraor- dinary protestations of affection with vehemence, she kept him at a distance. On Tuesday the man went out to a café and returned home after drinking heavily. He went into his mother-in-law's room and again made proposals of marriage to her. As she refused, he took a revolver out of his pocket, and, follow- ing her out of the room from which she Bed with terror, he fired three times at her. The woman fell dead at the bottom of the stairs of the house, having been struck in the head. The murderer then turned his weapon on him- self, and inflicted two wounds in his chest and ribs, a third shot having missed. After that he pulled himself up to an adjacent window and' threw himself out. He was picked up bleeding and insensible, but not dead, and was conveyed to the hospital, where he now lies hover- ing between life and death. - -

THE CASs CASE: PROSECUTION OF P.C. ENDACOTT. —At the Bow-street Police Court, London, on Mon- day, Mr. Grain made an application for a summons for corrupt and wilful perjury against P.C. Endacott in con- nection with the arrest of Miss Cass. With regard to the witness Pietra, who had given evidence at the inquiry, some inquiries had been made, and the results were of an extraordinary character. The matter might develope into prosecutions for perjury again-t several persons. —Miss Cass, who was dressed in black, then attested as to the truth of the evidence she had given at the inquiry, and Miss Scott and Mr. Walford, the two other witnesses, did likewise as to their previous statements.—Mr. Vaughan said he had come to the conclusion that he would grant the summonses asked for, and the hearing of the case would come on next Tuesday, at 12 o'clock. —The Lord Chancellor has called upon Mr. Newton to submit to him in writing any statement he may desire to make in justification of his conduct, in the Cass case. The Lord Chancellor's inquiry relates exclusively to the conduct of the magistrate, and is entirely distinct from that being carried forward by the law officers of the Crown, which deals exclusively with the conduct of the policeman,

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.
A man named Cornelius Neill was killed on Cork Quay on Saturday, owing to the explosion of a barrel of whisky, to Which some boys had set fire with a match.
A farmer named Custy -was fired at on Sunday after- noon, at Ermaghmore, near 'Ennis, and, it is stated, was fatally wounded. The outrage was agrarian.

A Killarney telegram states that Mr. Buckley, vice- president of the Killarney National League, has been granted 30s. a -week for a month by the guardians, on account of his being an evicted tenant. - -

On Saturday an attempt was made to wreck the day mail on the Irish Great Northern Railway, near the 'Cillich Station, by placing large stones on the line at the same spot where '3O years ago a train containing the Earl of Enniskillen and other Orangemen was thrown off the line by a similar outrage, and the engine driver and another were killed, the passengers having a miraculous escape. The 'house of Michael Cahir, an extmsive farmer of 'Ballybone, was fire,i into on Monday night by moon- lighters, the shot! coming through the parlour window, shattering a lamp into fragments, and striking Mrs. Cahir in the face. The farmer recently discharged a herdsman from his employ, and this is -the supposed reason for the outrage. No clue to the perpetrators has been found. _ _

Mr. Blaine, the Republican candidate at the last election for the Presidency of the United States, has arrived in Dublin from Belfast, with his wife and 'daughter, after sojourning in Perth with his counntry- man, Mr. Andrew Carnegie, proprietor of the great American steel manufactory. He purposes spending some time in Ireland, to have a quiet look round, in order to see for himself the condition of the country. In a few days he will proceed onth, visiting cork and Kit. larney. Quartermaster Armitage, Sixth Brigade North Irish Division Royal Artillery, stationed at Dungannon, com- mitted suicide on Monday. He had been ordered to see the commanding officer; but, instead, he went to a druggist's and purchased some cyanide of potassium, which is used for cleaning gold lace, and drank a glass- ful, dying a few minutes afterwards. He had previously -written a note to his wife, saying that he had committed a serious crime, and could not meet the commanding officer.

In the Vice-chancellors Court, Dublin, on Saturday, a suit involving £250,000 was heard. A merchant, named James Carlisle, formerly of Belfast, died sometime since, leaving a very large amount of property. There were a number of claimants, the principal one being Mrs. Cherry Moore, a woman 75 years of age, the wife of a labourer living in :New Brunswick, who claimed, as sister and nearest relative of the deceased, to be entitled to the bulk of the property. The executors having ex- pressed themselves satisfied as to her identity, the Vice- Chancellor said there was no occasion to make further inquiries, and, on the application of her counsel, a sum of £5OO was allowed to her on account of the enormous fortune to which she was entitled.

On Monday, an extensive fire broke out in the Chandler's premises of Messrs. Lambert, Bryant, and Co., Grafton-street, Dublin, and owing to the inflam- mable nature of the contents spread rapidly. The fire I eventually communicated itself to the adjoining premises of Mr. Robinson, photographer, and the whole block of buildings, including Mr. Gertz's jewelry establishment, the Singer Sewing Machine Company's warehouse, a public-house, and a pianoforte warehouse, were more or less destroyed. Business in Grafton- street was entirely suspended. The fire brigade soon. arrived, but, abandoning all hopes of saving the burning building, devoted their attention to stop- ping.the fire from spreading to the adjoining premises. In a short time barrels of oil began to explode. The flames gradually became fiercer and fiercer till one by one all the floors had fallen in. At half-past three the brigade had the fire greatly under control. The damage done was very great.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY FACTION FIGHT.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY FACTION FIGHT.

An excursion on Sunday of Irish National Foresters from Belfast to Portrush was productive of terrible re- sults, a minister and two other persons being shot, and the train in which they journeyed to the latter place being completely wrecked. It appears that the excur- sionists, to the number of about a thousand, left Belfast I in two special trains about nine o'clock in the morning Ito spend their annual holiday at Portrush. On arriving at that town they were met by a crowd of Orange- 'men, and serious rioting ensued, many people on both sides being inure"d with stones and bottles. I The town was in an uproar all day, and the respectable inhabitants, as well as many English and American visitors, fled to the houses to avoid injury or molesta- tion. The handful of polite in the place, however, suc- ceeded in preventing anything worse than broken heads. After spending some hours in Portrush, the excursionists left for Belfast, and it was on the home journey that the most serious part of the day's havoc was witnessed. In- telligence of what had taken place at Portrush seems to have reached most of the stations along the line, and as the trains were passing crowds which had collected along the railway stoned the excursionists, nearly all the car- riage windows being smashed. The excursionists retaliated with bottles and other missiles. At Ballymoney Station several shots were fired from the first train. One young man, a grocer's assistant, whilst crossing a bridge which spans the station, received a bullet wound in the chest. Similar scenes took place at all the stations between , Ballymoney and Ballymena, stones being thrown at the I trains and shots fired in return. At Ballymena a Pres- byterian minister named Dowds, whilst proceeding to his church to conduct Divine service, was shot in the leg, and a young man standing on the platform was severely I wounded. On the arrival of the trains at Belfast the ex- cursionists got into cars. They were pelted with stones by a band of Orangemen, and replied with empty bottles; but the police prevented a serious development of the disturbance in Belfast.

About a.m. on monaay, a man was seen ,co jump from Clifton Suspension Bridge into the river Avon. The body fell in mid-stream at high tide, and was sub- sequently recovered by some boatmen, who conveyed it to the Bedminster mortuary, where it was identified as that of a young man named Miller, a paperhanger by trade. This makes the twenty-fourth suicide since the bridge was opened in 1864.

In the Queen's Bench Division, on Monday, judg- ment was given in the appeal of a publican, who had been fined £3O and costs at Bow-street, at the instance of the Inland Revenue authorities, for diluting ale by mixing strong end small beer together. The Court upheld the conviction, Mr. Justice Grove remarking that if publicans were allowed to make a mixture of this kind there would be a considerable falling off in the revenue.
Dressmakers can buy no better sewing eotton than Bagley and Wright's, whtell for strength is unequalled.—Advt.

GREAT FIRES.—EXCITING SCENE. SEVEN MEN KILLED.—MANY INJURED. On Saturday evenin,. is fire was discovered on the extensive premises of Mr. Whiteley, in Bayswater, which have been the scene of destructive conflagrations several times within the past few years. On the present occa- sion, the disaster has been •attended with the loss of several lives and injuries of a severe character to many persons. The flames were first observed about seven o'clock, near the entrance to the packing shops and stores fronting Douglas-place. Or of Mr. Whiteley's exployes first discovered the fire, and immediately rang the fire alarm and connected the hose to hydrants, which are plentifully provided in the establishment. A fire escape and hose cart were soon on the scene, and no sooner was the hose got into play than a violent explosion nczurred. The roof and front walls of the cabinet factory were shat- tered, and before any of the firemen, policemen, nnd others who were directing their efforts to subdue the outbreak from Douglas-place could attempt to escape they were buried by a huge mass of bricks, iron, and timber. The fire escape, which was placed against the : wall of the burning building, and on which the firemen , were mounted, was Blown into several pieces. The I groans and shrieks of those buried beneath the d6bris , were painful in the extreme. Further lISSi..,`Ce had by this time arrived. The police at once work to rescue the sufferers, who were all, after considerable time, recovered and conveyed in cabs to the hospital. Valuable assistance was previously rendered by Dr. , Eccles, 30, Leinster-square, and Dr. Watson, Westbourne- grove. As the dead were got out, their bodies, which were frightfully mangled, were removed to Paddington Baths. Engines from West end and central districts arrived in rapid succession, and were followed by others from dis- tant stations. By 830 some 30 engines were on the spot, and a strong force of firemen directed their efforts to localising the fire by surrounding the burning pre- mises. The flames, however, gained such rapid head- way that they speedily penetrated through the building, and burst out in the front or pavilion within which were stored provisions, groceries, Zec. By ten o'clock the entire premises were glowing like a furnace. The roof of one of the departments fell in soon after ten o'clock, and 'several persons were buried beneath the debris, some being killed. Mr. Wrayson, superintendent of the Paddington Baths, was assisting a fireman to fix a hose against one of the buildings, when the wall fell, killing the fireman and injuring Mr. Wrayson. At 11 o'clock another wall fell, injuring two firemen. Ladder after ladder was raised against different parts of the burning buildings, and the firemen unflinchingly ascended to combat with the flames, until about midnight the officers of the brigade expressed the belief that they were about to gain the mastery of the fire, though to the ordinary observer the conflagration was at its fiercest. A man named Benjamin Woodger, who assisted in get- ting horses out of the stables early in the outbreak, narrowly, escaped being buried by a falling wall. No less than 80 jets were playing on the burning building. • It is known that the number killed is seven. The con- dition of some of the injured men is sericus. A search I of the ruins was attempted on Sunday, but had to be postponed until Monday. . Mr. Whiteley estimates the damage caused by the fire on his premises at Bayswater on Saturday at £525,000, and says that the amount for which he is insured is compara- tively trifling, Commencing with the outbreak in No- vember, 1882, six fires altogether have occurred on Mr. • Whiteley's premises. On the last occasion, in June. . 1885, four shops were burned out, and the loss was esti- mated at £350,000. In view of these facts it is not sur- prising to learn that incendiarism is believed to be at the bottom of Mr. Whiteley's heavy losses. I A tannery belonging to Mr. Booth, at Leek, was par- ' tially destroyed by fire on Saturday night. The damage is estimated at £2,000. Two fires broke out in Birkenhead on Sunday. The • first occurred in the house of Mr. William Sinclair Por- ter, Caroline-place, Claughton, and before the flames were extinguished damage to the extent of about £lOO was done.—At about six o'clock a fire broke out in the . , L loremises of Mr. J. Deeley, shoe dealer, Monk-street, Bir- , kenhead. The shop was gutted, and damage was done ' to the extent of several hundred pounds.

div.head: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.
div.p: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.

BLACKPOOL PIER. Aw've just come back fro Blackpool, un mi face is chippt an sooar ; Eawr fooak ull never know me, when aw put mi nooase th' door, For aw'm breawn as onny ouzel, an blistered here an theer, For th' owd sun's fairly frizzed me cat to Blackpool pier. When Lost aw med mi mind up, id wur weyvin rare un bad, Tin aw thowt a bit o' ocean air wed mek me weel an I glad; Soca off aw went to t' tackler, an aw sed, " Owd mon, look here, Aw'm beawn to scrat mi floats up on to Blackpool pier !" Aw towd mi mam, an hoo packt up—inside a carpetbag, A lot o' things—mi dicky, an mi fayther's Sunda tag; Wi corran cakes, an fatty uns, enoo to last a year; , An away then aw skeddadled off for Blackpool pier. Aw gript thad carpet bag o' mine, un swaggered like a ' lord, , Wi cooat o' glossy velveteen, an breeches woollen cord, Aw jogged reet deawn to t' station, an to t' tickut fella theer Aw sez, "Be sherp ! Third-class return for Blackpool ' pier."

When aw geet off at th' wafter side, aw stared wi gawpin een, For theer aw seed two iron brigs as t' watter rushed between Ut one o' th' brigs, aw axed a chap " Wod dosta co this here ?" He laft, an sed," Tha foo, it's nobbut Blackpool pier !" Aw hunted then for lodgings, an aw fun a likely place, An th' woman theer hoo welcomed me wi smiles o'l o'er her face. To mi tay awd hawf a dozen cakes an other hooamly cheer, For awd fun a hoss's appetite bi Blackoool pier. Aw weshed me then, an took a woke, for t' seea wur

gradely rough, On t promenade, until aw thowt awd raylee hed enuff. Feelin tired then, aw went to bed, while t' moon wur shinin clear, Then geet asleep, an dreamt o' neet o' Blackpool pier. I' th' mornin aw wur sleepy, an aw thowt awd rest misel, Sooa aw waited hawf asleep for t' knocker up, an t' factry bell; When o at once, t' thowt struck me, aw'r a foo for lyin theer, Deawn stairs aw went, an derled away tort Blackpool pier. Bud when aw geet aside o' t' pier, hey! ther wur sitch a creawd ; An theer aw seed a tackler wi a weyver lass fro th' Ewd, Sooa aw sheawts "Owd mon, ther'll be a row if t' wife shud ged to hear Tha wur wokin one o' th' weyvers eawt bi Blackpool pier!" An then he kicked up sitch a row, an swooar he'd breyk ml neck, For th' insult to his wife an kim ; aw kept mi tongue i' check, An soon " Owd mon, aw'll keep id dark," aw whispered in his ear, "If tha'll pay for a week's ticket on to Blackpool pier."

He wur fain to be let off so chep, an on aw went mong t' swells, As seemed to think as t' pier wur med for nobry bud thersels, Sum drawled eawt "Poor old chappie," others simpered " Tottie dear !" Aw laft at th' lot till aw wur sooar o' Blackpool pier! 0' t' seets aw see while aw wur theer, aw kordd attempt to tell, Aw wur seea sick, kicked wi t' donkeys, an wave- battered too—pell mell An aw wooar mi shoon eawt dancin—Hey, aw med sum wear an tear, 'Mong t' planks o' th' dancin platform on to Blackpool pier.

One neet aw'r gradely lonely—lookin reAwnd, whoa shud aw see Bud P—never mind her name, a lass as weyves aside o' me; Un we danced, an woked, an toked till id wur midneet very near, Bud nobry knows bud us wod passed o' Blackpool pier. Tin neaw aw've come back wi her, an aw'm owt bud fain we hey, For to-morn, or else t' day after, we've to stert o' bein t' slave; Bud this mitch neaw aw'll tell yo, aw believe awst gooa next year, WI a wife—an woke eawt arm in arm on Blackpool pier, JACK 0' ANN'S.

div.head: ALLEGED REitniitY BY A WIDNES
div.p: ALLEGED REitniitY BY A WIDNES
.GROCER.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Day, George Maddison. grocer, of Simms Cross, Widnes, was charged with having, on the 15th June, committed wilful and corrupt perjury on affidavit in an action in the High Court of Justice, Queen's Bench Division. Mr. M'Connell prosecuted, and Mr. Swift defended. In the action referred to, Mr. Knowles, provision merchant, Liver- pool, was the plaintiff, and Mr. Maddison was the defendant. The plaintiff was suing the defendant for about £26, alleged to be due for goods supplied. It seemed that certain boxes of bacon were stapplied from Mr. Knowles to Mr. Maddison, through a man named M`Grath, but the bill was sent direct to Maddison, who also communicated with Mr. Knowles about the matter. The alleged perjury was that in 3laddison's affidavit in the High Court of Justice he said—"l have at no time had any deal- ings with plaintiff, and have not at any time re- quested him to supply me with any goods, nor have 1 received any goods from him."—For the defence, Mr. Swift contended that at the time Maddison took the affidavit in question he was perfectly satis- fied that he knew nobody in the matter of buying this bacon but M`Grath. He gave the order to M`Grath, and received the goods, he believed, from 14`Grath. There was not a single word in the affi- davit untrue, when taken in the light of the evidence as it then stood. Mr. Swift further urged that the case had been brought into this court for the pur- pose of extorting money.—His lordship informed the jury that he did not think there was sufficient evidence to justify them in convicting the prisoner. The jury returned a verdict of "Not guilty.''—llia lordship said he could not too strongly condemn the practice of persons resorting to the criminal law for the purpose of getting their debts. This, his lord- ship thought, was a most improper prosecution, and. he should allow the prosecutor no costs.

The Lord Mayor of L----o-na-o-,-;.gave a banquet to her Majesty's Ministers on Wednesday night. Lord G. Hamilton, in responding to a toast on behalf of the navy. said that th e Admiralty had been able to send out the great fleets which had been engaged in the recent operations without drawing on the reserve at all. Lord Salisbury, in responding for Ministers, con- gratulated the Lord Mayor upon the office he held, as it was no slight honour to have been the Lord Mayor of the Jubilee Year of the most loyal people on the earth. The unbidden loyalty and enthusiasm would remain not only on the minds of the people of this kingdom, but also upon the minds of the distinguished visitors it was ourpleasure to receive. For Ministers the year had not been one of un- mixed festivities, especially for those who had the honour of sitting in the House of Commons. He must say that the House of Commons had been afflicted by its ancient malady the maxi- mum of garrulity and the minimum of legislation. He was afraid if this continued people would express their feelings in a hasty and unpleasant manner. This particular difficulty had gone on increasing year by year; but within the limits which this malady has imposed, the House of Commons had treated ministers with great confi- dence. The reason of the existence of the Govern- ment was to carry out the mandate of the country to resist all proposals of separation. He was glad to say that the House of Commons had recognised its duty in giving its first care to the condition of Ireland. Ministers had obtained the sanction of the House of Commons for dealihg with exceptional crime. They had to deal with a population no longer free, and they had proposed the remedy they thought best for the evil. There was no taint of unconstitutionalism on the measures they had • passed, and the responsibility for the use of those powers lay with the Government. Up to the pre- sent time they had been unable to repress crime ax they wanted, but now they felt that Parliament had • a right to ask the Government to use those powers to the best of their ability, and they would have a right to come upon them with heavy censure if the weapons with which they had entrusted the Government failed in their effect. This trouble was the result of the strange depres- sion of affairs, which was felt even in the City. When men were prosperous measures succeeded; when times were depressed the best measures failed. The Government did not conceal from themselves that it was in the greater prosperity of the two nations that they hoped for a renewal of the sym- pathy which should exist. He could not pass by the agricultural position in the country. He did not say that the Government could give the re- lief wanted to the agricultural population, but he could not help expressing his deep sympathy for them. With regard to foreign affairs, he referred • with satisfaction to the fact that the last subject of difference between the Russian Government and I ourselves, which referred to the Afghan frontier, had been settled, and in a manner satisfactory to both Governments. The matter had been settled in a way that was in the interests of both Governments, for there was plenty of room there for both Governments, for two centuries to come. With respect to Egypt peculiar obligations were im- posed on us. By our own act we went to i that country, and if we left it, t would be left a prey to anarchy or to other Powers. That fact had im- posed obligations on us, and that consideration was the dominant one in making a settlement; but while we were endeavouring to do • that, we had to con- sider other nations. The presence of English troops in Egypt was a trial to the feelings of many Alussul- mans and some Christians. The country knew what had taken place lately. The arrangement made with the Turkish Government had failed and was not to be carried into effect, but he hoped no one would imagine that because of that our former duty to the Egyptian people had lost anything of its solidity. We must not leave that country until lit was safe from interference from without or I within. The laws were being better observed in ! that country, and the state of the fellaheen was be- ing improved. Last November he discussed the prospects of European peace. A war on the Conti- nent of Europe was a calamity from which every one • shrank. Men practised in the conduct of European affairs had thought that peace could not be main- tained, but without prophesying he would venture Ito hope that the Lord Mayor would finish his tenure I of office in a state of profound European peace.
