div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, AUGUST 13, 1887.

IT is one of the maxims of the law that for every wrong there is a remedy, but in going into court to try to find the remedy the injured party too often comes out feeling that his last state is worse than his first, if this were not so frequently the case, we may be sure that a large number of people who suffer from nuisances of various kinds would gn to law with a view to getting rid of them. A farmer at St. Helens, named WHITFIELD, has been taking the bull by the horns, and he has got the better of the animal. He sued the St. Helens Copper Company for doing dam- aVe to his crops by the sulphurous fumes Which they emitted from their works; and, as he proved his case at the Liverpool ! Assizes on Saturday, the jury found a verdict , in his favour for £25. He was fortunate in i being able to bring the offence home to the , Offender; for it seems that there are other copper works near the farm. Had he been so hemmed in with them as not to be able to th Say of any particular sinner—" Thou art , d e man "—the chances are that the offen- ors would have escap-d Scot free. That, at r any rate, is how the matter stands at North- ii Wich ; everybody suffers from subsidence Caused by the salt works; but because it is Impossible to say which of the works is the cause of a particular injury there is no com- Pensation to be obtained. If the injury were Small and individual, there would be no diffi- kik_ cnity about securing damages; but as it is Pr' large and general nothing can be done—ex- ponder on the absurdity of the saying that "there is no wrong without a remedy." It is pretty much the same, we suppose, With the mischief caused by our filth-laden Streams and rivers. The nuisance is glaring, hut alas, where is the remedy? An effort is j3eing made to bring somebody to book for the horrible condition of Sankey Brook; and We trust it will be successful. St. Helens is thriving place; it has grown very fast; and 'runt the nature of its industries it is not over Clean. " Works " are to be respected. of °3ourse, but they should not be permitted to i ecome a nuisance to their neighbours. ,4 Works" help to keep the people alive; °Ut if existence is to be spent within the Itea of the odours of Sankey Brook, it Tay well be asked—ls life worth living ? he River Mersey is almost as foul --"" how foul it is during this hot Weather those who live near its banks t°o well know. There is a wonderful 1 .aoacity in the human system to adapt itself and make the best of, bad conditions. we find people living, after a fashion, `4 filthy hovels, to enter which would make ! Person instantly ill whose life is passed `ltinder average conditions. In the same way, wila.clse who live in the neighbourhood of the retsey have got used to it, or there would 431? g since have been an epidemic. But f Is bad at the best to be accustomed to a AcIIII atmosphere; and something ought to be °ne with a view to purifying the stream. It is, 10 be sure, a big job. Hercules had a heavy t,tder on hand when he undertook to clean Augean stables ; but the foul refuse he to deal with was as nothing to the filth it,ich runs daily down the River Mersey. ege Chairman of the Irwell Conservancy thernmittee has just published the results of the investigations of their inspectors as to is e Irwell and its tributaries. The summary , 40a truly appalling document. There are k less than 28 towns on the Irwell, the a_uolie, the Croal, the Irk, and the Medlock, 4ilcl with few exceptions, the authorities ate ta4 ItSing the streams as main sewers. Here tau extract or two from the report r— kli3,„i'n'T (oN THE luwELL).— Population, 52,128. I,44,years ago purchased land for sewage works at p 1 life, but, as yet 41885), nothing to prevent ion; house and closet refuse and the usual I.l„,_rers from works, and cinders, all are carried into th': through Elton and other brooks which pass `cgigh t 1 oto) re town. 111;4,114u (ON THE MEDLOCK). POlndatiOH, ksr=o. The same. 341,,rlotTEsTrat (ON THE InwELL).—Population, The whole sewage of the city, consisting fsetu°le drainage, water-closet refuse, and manu- Irk „ ring pollutions, passes into the rivers Irwell. exist'_°en_4l(l Medlock. Sch(mes on pa )er have been in „ nutte, ce tor a number of years they furnish Any. -,al for discussion at C0un....-etings occasion- t'- is filth of course passes into the Mer-

sey, and if a similar investigation was made as to the towns on the Mersey, it would be found that the case was as bad or nearly as bad. Bolton, however, does not pollute the river with its sewage, and why should not the rest of the towns on the Mersey and its tribu- taries be compelled to dispose of their refuse other than by tumbling it into the river? What has been done can be done, and if the people were properly alive to their own in- terests, they would rise in revolt against the abominatian which flows by their doors. , Granted that the evil is in some degree mitigated by the action of chemicals in des- troying some of the germs of disease. The condition of the river is still too bad to be patiently tolerated. Several prosecutions are, we are glad to see, being instituted ; and the Conservancy committee are to be commended on the course they are taking. The wrong is a terrible one; and, if there be a remedy, it should, at all costs. be found and applied.

THE nomination of candidates for the Northwich Division of Cheshire was held on Monday, and the voting takes place to-day, though it will be Monday next before the re- sult of the election will be known. It must he a trying thing for the candidates to be held in suspense for thirty or forty hours after the last vote has been recoided ; and. under or- dinary circumstances, there can be no ques- tion that it would be best to "have it over" as soon as possible. But Northwich is some- what notorious for rioting after the declara- tion of the poll, people's feelings during the balloting being worked up to a high pitch of excitement; and it has, therefore, been de- termined, on this occasion, to let Sunday in- tervene as a day of rest and of peace before Proceeding to the task of counting the votes. The election is regarded throughout the con- stituency, and indeed throughout the coun- try, as one of a most momentous kind. Should I Lord HENRY GROSVENOR secure the seat held by the late Mr YERDIN as a Liberal Unionist, it will be felt that this part of the country, at any rate, has not changed its mincl, on the question of Home Rule; and Lord HARTINGTON and his followers will be en- couraged in their opposition to the policy of Mr. GLADSTONE. On the other hand, if the victory be with the Liberals—if Mr. BRUN- NER be returned, as we trust he will be, by a large majority, it will be generally acknow- leged that Home Rule principles are in the ascendent, and that the voice of the country is against the Government. The Tories still try, at their various meetings, to frighten people by talking of disintegration and break- ing- up of the British Empire; but even the timidest of electors have ceased to be afraid of this bogey. Voters of all classes have, by a quick interchange of information and ideas, become familiar with the fact that Home Rule in the Colonies has not endangered the British Empire. They know, on the contrary, that disintegraticn would immediately set in if an attempt was made restrict the right of self-government. Canada, like Ireland, was ready to revolt until authority was given her to manage her own affairs. Give Ireland Home Rule to the extent that it has been con- ceded to Canada, and she will be as loyal to-morrow as Canada is to day.

But beyond the matter of securing Home Rule for Ireland, there are other questions in which the electors are interested; and they have ta ask themselves—the working-class electors in particular—whether they are as likely to get what they want from a Tory Administration as from a Government with , Mr. GLADSTONE at its head. The House of Lords requires to be either "ended or mended." Is Lord SALISBURY likely to lend himself to a task of this kind 1' It is about as reasonable to expect this as it is to expect the Archbishop of CANTERBURY to aid the Liberation Society. Then there is the ques- tion of the reform of the Land Laws—a question which goes to the root of things in their bearing on the social and material con- dition of the people of this country. Lord SALISBURY and Lord HARTINGTON are both landed aristocrats ; they and theirs have been living on "the fat of the land" for generations ; and they are not to be counted on to institute reforms which will thrust them in the back-ground, and perhaps com- pel them to disgorge some of their ill gotten plssessions. They may make a show of doing something, but what they do will be a sham, as witness the ridiculous attempt which is being made to make provision for Labourers' Allotments. As the bill stands, it is fenced with such conditions as will en- able any landowner who likes to snap his fingers at its so-called compulsory clauses. It is a mere make-believe, and unless it is radically altered it will prove to be as much of a dead letter as the much-derided Agricul- tural Holdings Bill of the BEACONSFIELD Government. As to temperance legislation, we know what the Tory idea is on that sub- ject. They will do nothing until they are compelled. The two candidates who are appealing to the electors of Northwich are fairly typical of the difference between Liberalism and Toryism on this subject. Mr. BRuNNER, when straight questions are asked as to whether he will vote for Sunday Closing and Local Option, gives straight answers ; if elected he will support both proposals. Lord HENRY GROSVENOR, when questioned, speaks with a very uncertain sound. He does not say that he is in favour of either measure; rather the contrary, for he sneers at anything which it is suggested should be done in this way as "patchwork legislation." He would leave the whole matter to be "included in the general measure of local government reform to be introduced next session." That is to say, a Tory Government can do just as it likes, and it will be all right to Lord HENRY GROSVENOR. This sort of answer will not satisfy the Temperance Reformers of the Northwich Division. They are in earnest, if his lordship is not, and they will, if we mistake not, vote to a man for the open- minded, straight-running Liberal candidate, and thus swell the large majority by which, it is confidently hoped, he will be returned to Parliament.

A WARRINGTON DIVORCN CASE.—In the Divorce Division, on Wednesday, Sir James Hannen had be- fore him the case of Hollowood v. Hollowood and Keeling. The petition was that of the husband, who resides in Manley-street, Warrington, a forge labourer, for a divorce by reason of his wife's adul- tery with the co-respondent, Mr. Mark Keeling, in the employ of the Strangeways Brewery Co. There was no defence. Mr. M‘Gasky appeared for the petitioner, who married the respondent in 1874 at the Registry-office, Tunstall. They afterwards went to live at Wigan, and ultimately at Warrington. There were two children of the marriage. In 1881 the co- respondent came to live at the petitioner's house as a lodger, and in 1885 Mr. Hollowood made a dis- covery upon which the case was based. He ordered the co-respondent away, but the latter refused to go, and turned the petitioner out of the house. (Laughter.) Subsequently the respondent and co- respondent went to live in Derby-street, Lower Broughton. His Lordship granted a decree nisi with costs. It may be mentioned that Mr. A, Browne, solicitor, Warrington, acted on behalf of the petitioner. Tat Le.wiaass's New Black Carrants.—sidrot,

div.p: .voßr rr TP7n-ri .Y! ,11R711`14_ Z 1 aHT - THE EX A.MINER, SATURDAY. AUGUST 13, 1887:
TOUCH AND GO." Another Rose Queen has been crowned at Earlestown. This surely will be the last rose of summer.
No more butterine ; mlrgarine 's the word. But what of that ? Sweet fat by any other name will taste as sweet.
The latest news from Paris is that a divorce has been pronounced between a deaf and dumb couple. Really, the way some people throw away chances of happiness is aston- ishing.

It is stated that two medical men appointed by the Court to examine the mental condition of Mooney, who recently attempted to set fire, at N.ew York, to the steamer Queen, have pronounced him insane. There is a fitness of things, in this instance, in a lunatic being called "Mooney."

The Government have done an illegal thing in appointing a sheriff of Lanarkshire who is not qualified to hold the office. Instead of backing out of a false position, they have plunged further in; they have positively in- troduced a bill to legalise the appointment. This is class legislation with a vengeance.

In the Marylebone district of London five persons in one family have been made seri- ously ill by using filtered " water. It trans- pires that the filter had acted as a receptacle for organic matter, which had begun to fer- ment in the hot weather. Moral : If you use filtered water, be sure that it is filtered ; keep your cleanser clean. A Parr collier, named Michael White, has been sentenced, at the Liverpool Assizes, to seven years' penal servitude, and twenty-five lashes, for robbing and assaulting a woman. Rascals of this kind require to be made to feel their punishment. The collier may be permitted to have his dog when he is well- behaved ; but when he becomes brutal it is the right thing to treat him to the "cat."

Police-constable Endacott is to be pro- secuted for perjury for the evidence given in connection with the Cass case. This is as it should be, but what a reflection it is on the original attitude of ' the Go- vernment ! Mr. Smith was right when, in the first instance, he said there was something more at stake than the character of the young woman, but he oid not think it would come to this. If he did, so much the worse for him in hanging back as to an in- quiry. Mr. N. S. Shaler, in an able article in " Scribner's Magazine,' says :—" The geo- logical record shows us clearly that, in the hundred million years which have elapsed since the plants and animals of the land have been in existence, the regions of the tropics have never been subject to frost," A hundred million years is a long spell; but it is not to be compared with a Coercion Bill which is for ever and ever. Still, one cannot help thinking how it will stand with that Coercion Bill at the end of a hundred million years.

Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. for the Widnes Division, does not seem to have much fear of the Corrupt Practices Act. On Saturday, he entertained from 1,200 10 1,500 of his " supporters and their friends" at his father's residence, Otterspool ; and we learn that " refreshments were served free of charge." The other day Sir W. C. Brooks ex • plained to certain "friends and supporters" that the law did not permit him to refresh them. Is there one law for Cheshire and another for Lancashire? Or is it that Mr. Edwards-Moss sets the law at defiance?

The result of the inquiry into the circum- stances of the death of Joseph Kay, labourer, of St. Helens, can scarcely be said to be satisfactory. He was fatally scalded through the boilernaan of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, turning steam into a sewer in which the de- ceased was at work. It does not seem that Makin, the boilerman, had had any orders on the subject, though he admits that one of the labourers had asked him not to turn the steam on without letting them know. The arrange- ment, so far as there was one, was of a most indifferent kind. The stable door will, of course, be locked now that the horse has been stolen.

Mr. R. A. Naylor, of Warrington, is jubi- lant. As he told his congregation at Thel- wall on Sunday, he has had the greatest honour of his life conferred upon him by being permitted to speak from the same plat- form as "a distinguished M.P., and a real live lord," while "a real lady " afterwards shook hands with him. Some men are born to greatness, some achieve greatness, but Mr. R. A. Naylor has had greatness thrust upon him, and he is supremely blest.
It seems Mr. Naylor has been speaking from the Tory platform at Winsford. He followed the "live lord" and the " distin-
guished M.P ," and by way of peroration he gave them a few lines "composed by him- self"—as follows:

Lord Henry's sure to have my vote, Let this be your decision; Then on the thirteenth he will be M.P. for this Division. After recovering from this outburst, Lady Henry Grosvenor shook hands with the man who thus promised his vote—it is usual to do so—and now Mr. Naylor is ready to black the boots of any person who can prove that he is related to "a real live-lord." Touching the few lines "composed by himself" we somehow suspected that our neu- tral contemporary has not reproduced the whole of them. Can this be a verse which has been omitted ? It is certainly after the
Naylor style:— Lord Henry is a nice young man, Beloved by great and small, And sure I am he'll be " returned " Safe back to Eaton Hall.

The Government dropped the bankruptcy clauses of the Irish Land Bill because they were shown to be so bad; but with a callous- ness which is disgraceful they have put noth- ing in their place. Mr. Dillon sought, on Saturday, to remedy this defect by ensuring that some provision should be made for deal- ing satisfactorily with arrears of rent; and Mr. Chamberlain ' and Sir Wm. Harcourt assisted him. But Lord Hartington put his foot down in a bold bad fashion ; and caused the amendment to be rejected. His lordship in this matter showed himself more Tory than the Tories themselves. He snubbed Mr. Chamberlain, too, and people are won- dering how much mare of this sort of thing the member for West Birmingham will stand.

llELsav HILL ON FrEß.—Some excursionist throwing a lighted match amongst the burnt heather and bracken, at Helsby, has set fire to tue hill, and it has been found impossible to extinguish the flames. The fire has burned down to the very roots, and seems destined, without a heavy rainfall, Ito clear all the vegetation off the hill, which is a celebrated Cheshire landmark.
LOCAL NEWS.

_ MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances whm they first find their eyesight fail- ing, they purchase all kinds of inferior manufactured spec- tacles which in the end cause their oyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deans,.at“, Manchester, and 143, Lord-street, Southport, has invented his" Perfection " Spectacles, which he adopts at either of the above addresses at 78 6d per pair. He will guarantee ' that they are not to be equalled in the country for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet
"How to preserve the sight " free on apolication.—Advt.

ISPNCORN I.IIRIAL BOARD —The monthly meetlng was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. Rugerson, and there were present Messrs Littler, Coleburn, and Sil- ktdd (clerk). it was reported that during the four months ended July 25 th re were 90 interments; corresponding patio(' last year 69. The fees received during the same period amount to £B9 18s 6d ; last year £95 19s 6d; decrease £d Is. ACCIDENT TO A CHILD AT WIDNES.—A child named Michael Tansey, aged two errs, son of Michael Tansey, Chemical labourer, Pitt-street, Widnes, was severely injured on Monday morning. The child fell in front of a horse and cart, and one of the luirse's hoofs struck him on the forehead, rendering him unconscious. Ha was carried home, and there attended by Dr. Hutchinson, under whose care he is progressing hlVOUrebly. POACHING AT NORTON —On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Thomas Cnorlton, was charged with poaching at Norton, m the 3rd August. Rally in the morning of the day named SergeantOldficld and Constable Jackson saw the defendant coming across the field. He had a trap in each hand, and several pegs smeared with fresh soil in his pockets. He admitted that he had " only been after a rabbit fine of 103 and costs 113 61 or in &twit 14 days hard labour. VISITORS TO BLACKPOOL EIIPAIId stay at the Station Tem- perance Hotel, tight opposite Central station. Central position. Commodious and accommodating. Terms easy. —Apply J. Heap.—Advt. - .

FIRE AT WlDNES.—Constables Worsfold and Houghton on 6unlay af cernoon discovered a fire in the cellar of the shop of Mrs Jamieson, earthenware dealer, Waterloo-road, Widnes. By promptly taking action they extinguished the flames by means of buckets of water. There was a large quantity of paper and straw in the cellar, and it is supposed that the material was Ignited by some person accidentally dzepplng a lighted match down the grid RS he passed. r SCENE IN A:RUNCORN LODGING-HOUSE.—At the Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Messrs J. Brundrit arr' James Handley, Martha Mclntyre was brought up in custody charged with as;aulting Sarah Aim Gibson, a lodging-house keeper, of Mersey-strest. Prisoner is a travelling hawker, and had been lodging at Gibson's house for some days past. On -Monday she was drinking with Caine companions, and a disturbance took place. Mrs Gibson interfered, and prisoner struck her on the head several times with either a spoon or a fork. The police were sent for, and prisoner left the house, but subse- quently returned, and buret the door open, and finished up by assaulting the complainant again.—She was sent to gaol for seven days with herd labour, without the option of a fine. THE TALK OF THE TOWN. Howell's Golden Herb

A LARGE GARDEN PARTY —On Saturday afternoon Mr. T. C. Edwards-Mess, M.P. fordbe Widnes Division, invited a large number of his supporteis and 'riende to a garden party at his father's teeidenee, Otterspool. Of the number present. conjectured at between 1,200 and 1,500, 400 were from Widnes. The day was beautifully fine, and the grounds attached to Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss's residence were greatly admired Mr. Edwards-Moss, M.P., received the visitors at three o'clock, the intervening time from then to dusk being spent in racing, or watching the running, indul- ging in the amusement of Aunt Sallies, etc, and rambling' about the grounds. Between four and eight refreshments I were served, free of charge. The Widnes Soap Works Brass Bend and the band of the Lancishire Yeomanry Hussars were in attendance, and discoursed music of an enjoyable charecter. The Hussars Band played for dencing. The I whole of the time was very pleasantly spent, and Mr. Moss's I liberality will not soon he forgotten. WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—The monthly meet- ing was held at the Town Hall yesterday. Mr. H Wade ' Deacon presided, and there were present Dr. OtKeeffe, Messrs R. H. Davies, S. Robinsen, S. Sadler, T. Sadler, E. I Carey, J. Mid wood, J. T. Allen (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian).—The Librarian reported that there were 845 borrowers on the register, and the total number of hooks is- sued during July was 3,482. The daily average issue was 134. The total number of readers in the reading TOOll WAS 11,204, and the average daily attendance 430. The fines paid during the month amounted to £l4s 31—It was de- cided to allow the librarian a fortnight's holiday, and it ' was also decided that in future the reading room and li- brary should be closed on bank holidays.—The Caairman pointed out that in other towns popular free lectures were given in connection with the free library, and he suggested that they in Widnes should follow their exemple. There was, however, nothing in the Libraries Act giving the com- mittee power to spend money for such a purpose, and it was decided that the clerk should write to Liverpool, Bir- mingham, dm, and ascertain how the expenses of the lec- tures were defrayed. WASTE OF WATER AT WIDNES.—Mrs Either Singleton, butcher, Vic'oria-road, was summoned before the Widnes magistrates, on Thursday, to answer a charge of wasting the water of the Local Board. Mr. J. T. Allen, the clerk, prosecuted. The Water Inspector paemed the premises at nine o'clock on the night of the 26th ult, and noticed water running to waste. Three hours liter he found that the escape of water WAS considerably greater, and the pavement outside the premieem was completely flooded. An inspec- tion revealed that there was a hosepipe attached to the tap in the plaughterhonee, and the water was running into a tub to overflowing.—ln reply t. Mr. Knowles, who defended,! the inspector said about 2 000 gallons of water would be wasted. The price was 61 per 1,000 gallons—The defence was that a man in Mr. Singleton'a employ had tried to oh. tam n water earlier in the day, but it was "shut off," and he had walked away without turning the tap busk. Hence the waste of water.—Mr. Brock said this was the excuse given in almost every instance. A fine of ss, and costs. Is Cel. was imposed --Samuel Merrina, builder, Was fined lOs and costs for using water for trade purposes which was only supplied for domestic use.—lt was proved by an inspector of the Local hoard that one of the defendant's men obtained water from a cottage in Moor-street for the purpose of make lug mortar. THE MANUFACTURE OF " SAVOURY DI7CES '2 AT WIDNES. —Before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, George Davideon, butcher, and purveyor of potted meats, Ann-street, was summoned for exposing for sale meat which Was unfit for human fool. —Mr. Allen. clerk to the Local Beard, prosecuted, and stated that the importance of nsing wholesome food in the preparation of potted meat could not be overestimated as once the ingredients were mixed it would be impossible to trace them afterwards. On the 14th July Inspector Dick- son called in the defendant's shop and saw two pieces of ' decomposed meat exposed for sale. The meat was quite unfit for food. The defendant's wife expressed sorrow, and said it was "cat's meat." The meat was not, however, lakelled to dietinguish it from any of the ether meat in the shop, The meat was afterwards examined and was condemned by a magistrate.—A man gave evidence as to the manufacture of the potted meats which, be said, ware composed of liver, lights, and melt.—A "savoary dock" was handed up to the magistrates for inspection, much to the amusement of the persons in court.—Mr. W. Boyle, solicitor, of St. Helens. who defended, contended that the meat was only intended for consumption of cats, and he called two persons who stated they had purchased some on the day in question for their cats—The defendant, had been fined £5 in 1880 for a similar offence, and he Was now ordercd to pay a like amount, together with costs, £1 Os 63. —Mr. Boyle gave notice of appeal.

Denis Glancey, a chemical la- bourer. who resides at Moss Bank, and Anthony Burke. a boy, whose boats is in Victoria-road, were charged with etealing a pigeon, value Is, the property of James Hot, e greengrocer, Ann-street Glancev was also charged with atm.& log Houle. It appeared that on Saturday night Mrs fools had a cage containing five pigeons in the market. During a brief absence from her charge, one of the pigeons was stolen. LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY.—The proprietors of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Rail- way held their hundred and second half-yearly meeting on Wednesday,under the presidency of the newly-elected chairman, Mr •G. J. Armytage. In moving the adoption of the report, the chairman said that the receipts for the past half year had ex- ceeded by over £lOO,OOO those of the corresponding six months, while the working expenses had in- creased by £35,333. The report was adopted, and a dividend at the rate of 31 per cent per annum was declared. , -A RUNCORN DIVORCE CASE. In the Divorce Division, on Thursday, Mr. Justice Butt had befOre him the case of Hulme v. Hulme and bole. The petition was that; of a husbaud, an auctioneer, of Runcorn, for divorce by. reason of his wife's adul- tery with the co-respondentsa fruit dealer, of Middlewi ch. There was no defence. The marriage took place so far back as 1837, at Burslem, and in that town they lived for many years, there being six children of the marriage. Sixteen years ago they separated, and in 1882 she went through a ceremony of marriage with the co-respondent, Jos. Hoole, who was called in support of the petitioner's' case. He stated that she at the time represented that she was a widow, but four years ago he found' that ihe was married, and he left her. His lordship granted a decree nisi, but Made no order as to costs. - Tin SHIP CANAL AND THE BRIDGE WATER NiVlGA'rrorr COMPANY.—A meeting of the proprie- , tors of the Bridgewater Navigation Company was ' held at Manchester on Wednesday, to appoint liquidators to voluntarily wind up the company in consequence of its purchase by the Manchester Ship Canal Company. Mr. J. W. Cropper, chairman of the directors, presided. A discussion* was raised with reference to the surplus amount to be appor- tioned among ordinary and preferential share- holders. On the motion of the Chairman, it was resolved "That the company be wound tip volun- tarily under the provisions of the Companies Acts, 1862 and 1867, and that J W Cropper, N Buckley, J A Kendrick, J. W. Madam, M.P., Sir F. Mappin, M.P., ' and Thomas Roberts be and are hereby appointed liquidators for the, purpose of such winding up." The Chairman stated that the capital would be re- paid to the shareholders at the earliest possible date. With regard to the surplus an equitable distribution would be sought. Since the purchase by the Ship Canal Company of the Bridgewater Canal, posters, on which the following is printed, have been posted at the various wharfs :—" Manchester Ship Canal Company (Bridgewater Canals undertaking.") The names upon the hurries have also been changed. ANOTHER "ROSE QUEEN" CORONATION AT EARLESTOWN.—The neighbourhood of Haydock- street and Market-square, Earlestown, had an ani- mated appearance on Saturday afternoon, when some interest was excited by the crowning of a rose queen. Mrs Brown, Mrs Tatham, and other residents of the vicinity had arranged the interest- ing ceremony, which was witnessed by a large number of persons. About half-past two o'clock a procession of children was: formed, various charac- ters being pourtrayed by the attire of the children. Master John James Gorse wastrumpeter, Miss Ruth Uren officiated as crown bearer. and she was fol- lowed by the rose queen, Miss Violet Brown; her majesty's train-bearers being Miss Emily Statham and Miss Susie King. Immediately following. were two maids of honour, Miss Elizabeth Eilmmster, who carried the sceptre, and Miss Fannyjlall, who carried a basket of flowers. Next follovired the seasons, .as represented by Miss J. E. Statham (Spring), carrying an attractive basket of fruit; Miss Elizabeth Holcroft (Summer), with a splendid basket of flowers; Mitts Elizabeth Hall (Autumn), with a bunch of grain: and Miss Florrie Statham (Winter), who held in her hands a basket filled with a clever imitation of snow. The children walkeyl along Haydock-street into Cross-lane, and on returning went along Back Market-street and Oxford-street to Haydock-street, where, near Mrs Brown's house, the coronation took place. Miss Ruth Uren,- as the crown bearer, performed the in- teregting ceremony, and afterwards, on behalf of the other children and residents in the neighbour- hood,presented a handsome copy of the Bible to "Her Majesty," which was gracefully- acknow- ledged. All the processionists and some friends afterwards sat down to a pleasant tea at Mrs Browne's, and the children afterwards spent the afternoon in various games, amusements, &C. ROYAL JUBILEE EXHIBITION.—The number of visitors to the Exhibition on Thursday was 26,843, making a total since the opening of 2.195,125. The children who are being brought up under the aus- pices of the East Lancashire Systematic Masonic Educational and Benevolent Institution visited the Exhibition an Thursday. Dinner and tea were previded for them and their friends at the Temperance diffing-rown. They presented a cheer- ful, healthy appearance, and seemed greatly to enjoy themselves. ' PENKETE DAY AND gIINDA.TSCHOOLS.—The open- ing services in connection with the day and Sunday schools, held on Sunday, when two serinons were preached.in the Wesleyan Chapel by the Rev. E, O. Coleman, formerly of Warrington. In the afternoon at 230, the sacred cantata entitled The choicest gift" was rendered very efficiently by the choir, teachers, and friends, the connective readings- be- ing given by Mr. R. Cook. The work of re-budding the schools has been well carried out by Mr. J. Lloyd, Warrington, the painting, glazing, and plumbing being satisfactorily executed by Mr. John Mainley. There is now ample accommodation for , the scholars. There were good congregations at all the services, , and the collections amounted to £lO 5s 2d. , IloNouniNG A RUNCORN POET.—Prior to the proceedings in the Albert Hall, on Wednesday, the Gorsedd was again held near the Magazine in Hyde Park, Clwydfardd (the Archdruid) _presiding Mr Lewis Morris, M.A., author of the " Epic of Hades," and the "Jubilee Ode," which has been set to music by Sir Arthur Sullivan, introduced to the bardic fraternity present Mr P. M. Jones, a Welsh poet re- siding in Runcorn, and announced that that gentle- man had written a meritorious ode in honour of the jubilee. Mr Morris recommended the Gorsedd to take special notice of Mr Jones—a request which was readily granted, the degree of Ovate being con- ferred upon him. The Rev John Hughes, Welsh Wes- leyan minister, London—known in bardic circles as " Glanystwyth "—received the higher degree of Druid, after which the proceedings terminated. _ .

div.head: STOCKS WHLL PUMPING STATION.
div.p: STOCKS WHLL PUMPING STATION.

In moving-in7;do-p-tro-n-piii.HT-miiit7t-is-Coi the Gas and Water Committee, Mr. Brown said the engines at Stocks Well, recently altered, were working in the same satiefac- tory manner as they were on the day of the inspection. The speed of working at present was 64 strokes per minute, but the ultimate speed would be 81 strokes per minute. The water was now drawn from a hundred feet lower level than previously, and some difficulty had been experienced in working the pumps, and it was thought better at present to work the engines at a slow speed for a couple of months. The water was as near as possible quite clear, and there was being pumped soopoo gallons more than with the old pumps The water delivered during the past four weeks was 70 million gallons, which was a very large increase Upon wbat was delivered before. They could not have pumped that quanity of water unless they had made the alterations to the engines.—The minutes were approved.

Handley said he observed that West Bank Promenade was finished and he wished to know whether any seats were to be placed there—Mr. Wright pointed out the trouble and expense the Lugsdale sewer was to the Local Board through being continually opened and cleaned, and he sug- gested that the committee should urge upon the railway company the necessity of opening the new road and of mak- ing that pat t of the sewer they had to make.—Mr. Carey, in reply to Mr. Brown, said formerly Welsh blue bricks had been used in the gullies, dm, and these bricks were more expensive than Roughdale bricks. He did not quite understand how Mr. Brown got the amount of £5OO. Common bricks were very undesirable in places where they were exposed to changes of dry and wet. With re- gard to the promenede it was proposed to put down about 12 seats —ln reply to Mr. Wright, Mr. Carey said they should push on with the sewerage scheme as rapidly as pos- sible in order to put the town into a more healthy condition. —Mr. Taylor said Mr. Brown must have got hold of the wrong end of the stick. Previously the brickwork had been nine inches, having a layer of common brick under a layer of blue brick. Therefore a saving of money would be effected —Mr. Brown said he understood they were pat- ting in Roughdale brick where common brick would do.— The minutes were passed. HEALTH STATISTICS. The Medical Officer (De. Cooper) reported to the Health Committee that during July there were 103 births and 77 deaths, being at the rate of 41.2 and an 8 per 1.000 respec- tively. There were 26 deaths amongst children under 1 year, and 28 deaths amongst children between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused 24 deaths—The Nuisance Inspector reported that during July there had been eleven deaths from measles, one from typhoid fever, and eleven from diarrhoet and dysentry. compel property owners to alter their property in the man- ner recommended. If so it was a very serious item to alter all the closets in Widnes.—Mr. Carey asked for information as to the prevalence of sneasl.s. He suggested that the cloak rooms of the schools should have some disinfectants placed there as a prevention of disease.—Dr O'Keeffe said the property had only to be altered where a nuisance ex- isted Where there was not any nuisance the Board did not intend to tike any action. The Lord Mayor of Dublin, Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., contributes to his paper, the "Nation," of Friday, some lines on the Crimes Act. The produc- tion is based on the press announcement that all the 32 counties of Ireland are now proclaimed un- der various sections of the Crimes Act, and the first verse is as follows : • This is our thereof the Jubilee bounttis. A measure the vilest our land ever ea*, Placing each one of our thirty-two counties Under the scope of au infamous law. Will they submit to this act of atrocity? Will they be crushed by this cowardly blow? Will they be frightened by fory ferocity? Ireland speaks out, end ner answer is " No." Dublin will stamp on ; Wicklow will tramp on it; Kerry will drag it about through the mire; Limerick will batter it ; Waterford tatter it Wexford will bundle it into the fire.

div.head: FRIGiITFUL RA lIN AY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA. 200 PERSONS KILLED.
div.p: FRIGiITFUL RA lIN AY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA. 200 PERSONS KILLED.

Another frightful railroad disaster was, on Thurs- day, added to the list of those which have gone be- fore. A train of twelve coaches, loaded with excur- sionists, was that morning passing through Illinois. bound for the Niagara Falls. ear Chatsworth, a small town some hundred miles south of ,Chicago, the train had to cross a bridge, which spans the Vermillion River. This bridge was of wood, and the "stringers," or girders, consisting of long beams of timber, laid longitudinally beneath the metals, had apparently been weakened by recent prairie fires. However, from whatever cause, the bridge was unable to support the train, and as the crowded cars rolled over it. the beams gave way with an awful crash, hurling the unhappy excur- sionists amongst the wreck of the cars in a writhing heap below. The loss of life is terrible. Soon after noon seventy mangled corpses had been recovered. No fewer than 150 persons are injured, many of them having frightful fractures and contusion. A New York telegram, of Friday's date, says that the village of Chatsworth and Piper City, which are near the scene of the disaster, are compared to mortuaries by those who have visited the Spot. The railway stations, engine-houses, and public halls are filled with the dead, and the private houses all con- tain wounded persons. When the victims were re- moved from the wreck they were first laid in the adjacent cornfields. Many of the bodies were fear- fully mangled, and in some cases quite unrecog- nisable. The streets are filled with anxious persons seeking for their friends. Many pathetic incidents in connection with the accident are recorded. It is narrated that one poor man, whose legs were broken insisted that his wife and child should be removed from the debris before any help was ren- dered to himself. It proved that his child was dead, and his wife expired afteirbeing placed in the corn- field. The unfortunate husband was shortly laid beside her body, and then drawing a revqlver he committed suicide. It is considered probable that the bridge was set on fire by a spark from a passing engine early in the night, the dryness of the season having made the woodwork mere tinder.

A"Pimes" second edition telegram,-dated Phila- delphia, Friday, says that 110 bodies have been taken out of the wreck. The latest report states that fully 200 were killed. A son of the Rev. Mr. Snedecker, of Abington, 12 years of age, was found clinging to the corpse of his mother, with one of his legs and an arm broken, and suffering, in addition, the 'excruciating pain produced by the loss of an eye. He refused to take some brandy which was offered to him, asking in vain for water. The searchers came across several headless bodies, as well as bodiless heads, belong- ing, perhaps, to dear friends, or, at any rate to ac- quaintances It is painfulto relate that some of the residents of the vicinity plundered the corpses with wolfish avidity, but then others exerted themselves to the utmost to give aid and comfort to the suf- ferers. The schoolhouse, the church, and some of the private dwellings of the town of Chatsworth ' were used as hospitals, and everything which sur- gical skill and tender nursing could do to prevent further loss of life was done, not without consider- able success. Some of the bodies are mangled be- yond recognition, and in not a few cases several members of one family have perished. A telegram from the scene of the terrible acci- dent says that the disaster surpasses in its appall- ing extent any railway accident recorded in the history of the country. Two engines were attached to the train, which consisted of six day and six sleeping carriages, together with three cars for luggage. There were 960 passengers—all excur- sionists. The train left Bloomington early on Wednesday night. The bridge through which the train fell was an ordinary wooden trestle structure, erected over a ditch 10ft. deep and 15ft. wide. On nearing the bridge the engine-driver discovered it was on fire, but was unable to stop the train. The first engine Crossed over safely, and thenthe bridge fell. Tne second engine and some of the carriages were wrecked, some telescoping the others. The sleeping carriages remained on the track, bat were in great danger owing to the wrecked por- tion of the train having caught fire from the burn- ing bridge. There has been a prolonged drought in the prairie, and consequently water was unobtainable ; but the able-bodied survivors, with an ingenuity which did them credit, extinguished with dust the flames that enveloped the ruined train.

TRAP ACCIDENT.--About hal-pot five on Monday after- noon, AEI Mr. Collinson, of Ingle Dene, Overton, was driving along. Church-street, Frodsham, the horse was suddenly startled by the whistle of a railway engine, and bolted. Mr. Col linson and the coachman (who was sitting behind) were thrown violently out. The horse went up the Station-lane, collided with the Railway Company's horse and lorry, do- ing mach damage, and was caught just as it was crossing the line in front of an approaching train. The horse and the occupants of the dogcart sustained very little injury. EXTRAORDINARY FISHING.—An extraording fishing match has taken place between a party of gentlemen, eight in number, from Kingsley and Frolsham. The fishing COM. menced in the well-known pool belonging to the pro- prietor of the Red Lion Inn, Little Budwortb, at nine o'clock a.m , and finished at seven o'clock D M., on Tuesday last. They caught the large number of 555, eonsieting of perch, roach, and dace—a most excellent day's sport. They had four boats containing two fishermen with single rod only, and caught as follows :—No. 1 boat, 187; No. 2, 71 ; No. 3, 123; and No. 4, 174. The water was some- what " billowy," though a rather stiff breeze was blowing all day.

TECIINICAL EDUCATION AT FRODSIIAM BRIDGE M ILL.— During the past winter months the men employed at the Frodsham Bridge Mill met together and devoted one even- ing each week to the study and discussion of the new and Improved methods of manufacturing sour by . the roller , System, as now carried on in all the principal mills in the kingdom. In consequence of the knowledge acquired by this means, together with their practical work, seve,al of the most efficient entered their names as candidates for ex- aminations in milling. conducted under the auspices of the City and Guilds of i Londou Institute for the Advancement of Technical Education, held n May last. The report just published—this week—shows that the first prize of .£3 and Silver medal, the bronze medal, one first class and one se- cond class certificates, ordinary grade, have been awarded to four of the young men employed at the above mill.

"Dear sir,—lt is evident that Lord Henry Grosvenor has not the smallest knowledge of the subject on which, as I learn from you, he speaks. Let him show when (1) I was party to a perpetual 1 Coercion Bill for Ireland, or (2) to a bill creating new crimes out of what were not crimes (as Justice Holmes admitted), or (3) to a bill denying to Irish- men in respect to combination rights given 'co Englishmen, or (4) to a bill founding judic:ol tences.on the judgment of the Lord Ititeant, all of which is done by the late A,.:•;-falaely called a Crimes Act. E. GLA.DSTONE." MR. BRUNNER'S CANDIDATURE. LIBERAL MEETING AT WESTON. An open air meeting in support of the, candidature of Mr. J. T. Brunner, was held at Weston. on Saturday afternoon, Mr. James Handley, J.P., presided and there was a good audience. The Chairman said the question the electors were asked to decide was whether the Liberal Unionists and Conserva- tives combined should rule the destinies of tnisgreat empire, or whether they (the electors) would support their friend , Mr. Brunner, who had served them so well in the past and was ready and willing to support the just and the honoura- ble policy of their great leader Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) In supporting Mr. Brunner they declared themselves in favour of a righteous cause. (Cheers) The best settlement of the Irish question, upon which issue this election was be- ing fought, was to place trust in the Irish people (hear, hear)—and it was to the interests of the masses of the people of this country that the question should be settled as speedi- ly as possible, in order that domestic reforms, in which they all were deeply interested might be taken in hand (Cheers.) It was untrue that the Liberal party were in favour of dis- union ; they were the true Galenists, because they wished the Irish people to be in close sympathy with those of Eng- land, heart beating with heart. (Cheers.) Mr. Dunbabin moved. and Mr. Barrett seconded, a resolu- tion hailing with satisfaction the marked change in public opinion as evidenced by the recent election, and pledging the meeting to make the change more mark?d by returning to Parliament Mr. Brunner, a tried and ardent reformer. Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P.. supported the motion. The aim of the Tory party, he said, and of their youthful repre- sentative in this conte,:t was to poison the minds of the peo- ple against Home Rule for Ireland and to create passion and prejudice against the Irish nation. They did not do this because they felt deeply the proposals of Mr. Gladstone with regard to Ireland, but because they detested and hated with an undying hatred the great Liberal leader whose life had been devoted to building up the rights and interests of the people as opposed to the privileges of the aristocracy, the chief of which class they had to contend with in this election. (Cheers ) The simple question was, were the electors on the side of the people, or were they going to es- pouse the cause of the dukes and marquises? (Cheers.) This was the first contest in which the masses and the classes had come to close csarters. (Hear, hear.) He knew of no nobility by birth. The only nobility he recog- nised was the nobility of life, of labour, of good works, and a career devoted to the advancement of mankind. Ho would bow to no man who was acconnted noble simply be- cause he was his father's son. (Cheers.) What Commu- nity of interest had the working claEses with the class with which Lord Henry Grosvenor was associated ? ("None.") LIBERAL MEETING AT RUNCORN. SPEECH BY MR. WADDY, One of the most enthusiastic meetings ever held in Runcorn took place in the Publio Hall on Saturday evening. Mr. Sexton M.P., had been annonnoed to address the electors, but he did not put in an appear- ance, and the principal speaker was Mr. S. 1). Waddy, M.P. In an eloquent speech, of upwards of an hour's duration, he described some instances of great injus- tice done by landlords to their tenants, and concluded with an eloquent appeal on behalf of Home Rule. With one accord the crowded audience sprang to their feet, and, frantically waving hats and handker- chiefs, continued to cheer for several minutes after Mr Waddy had resumed his seat. In the absence of Mr R Shaw, Mr James Handley, J.P. occupied the chair, and on the platform were Mr S D Waddy, M.P., Mr W Abraham, M.P. MrW Croefield,;Mr C M Percy, the RevJ D Thomas, Dr O'Keeffe, Dr Hutchinson, Messrs J R Frith. 8 0 Beckett, B Kniyeton, J N T Clegg, R Norman, J W Carlile, T Handley, W Handley, J Jepson, R Pierpoint, R Forrestet, J D Jones, J Unaworth, J Littler, &o. The Chairmen' Mr. B. Kniveton, and Mr. W. Crosfield having delivered brief addresses on the question of the hour, Mr. S. D. Waddy, Q C., M.P., who was heartily cheered, said he had come with one message as he knew perfectly well that the one great question they had to consider was the question of Ireland. The Liberal Uaionists said they wanted to preserve the Union. He believed them entirely. But he, too, and other Liberals wanted to preserve the Union—(cheers)—and he claimed, as an English gentleman that they should believe him entirely. Therefore when a man said to him "I am a Liberal Unionist and you are a Separatist," he begged leave to say in perfeet good humour but with perfect plaieness. that that was an offensive and impertinent misrepresentation. (Cheers.) The two sides differed as to the way in which it should be done. He be- lieved as firmly as he believed in his existence that Mr. tatrat.rarn, as an Irishman, wanted to preserve the Union. (Cheers.) Hs believed that Mr, Abraham WAS 49 honest in the Matter as he (Mr. Waddy) wall, and if he was not, he would not shake hands with him as he did now. (Loud cheers.) There were two views as to how the mat- ter should be settled, and the question of the hour was which of these two views would the Northwich Division support. He was there to persuade there that the right view to support was this, that they could govern Ireland by simply keeping her down and choking her, and that the only way they conld govern her was to govern her by affection, by freedom, by equality, and by love. (Cheers.) The Conservatives said they had tried coercion year after year, and they had nothing else to give. The Irish people asked that their Parliament, which was taken from them by fraud, should be restored. The best and wisest statesmen of that time said that to rob Ire- land of her Parliament was not only wrong but stupid, and that in doing so they were sowing the seeds of discord, and would reap a red harvest of wrath and war and blood. And it had been true. From that time thore had been risings of the Irish people. Every now and then they had done that which no man was entitled to do, but that which all men had done in the agony of their struggles for freedom and for what they believed to be their rights. Now, with an almost unanimous voice the Irish people asked that their Parliament should be restored • and what would the Eng- lish people say in answer? The Tories and Liberal Union, lets said in effect that they would not agree to that, becausei the Parnellites were such ruffians, such murderers. All ' that sort of thing, if it were not shameful, would be simply amusing and absurd. This cry of " Parnellism and crime"- was the stock-in-trade of some people when they could not find an answer to an argument. They said, "I don't care about your argument; you're a thief." (Laughter.) The contention of the Irish people was that such a system of Ilandlord tyranny and rack•renting in Ireland had toads the I I question of land the central question in politics to them, and. that never could it be put right until they had such a I representative system that their representatives should not be outvoted by 400 to 100. There was only one way of getting at the truth, and that was to go and look. He (Mr. Waddy) went to investigate recent evictions, and he heartily wished it possible kr every voter in North wich Division to have seen what he saw within the last month or two. His ward for it that there would be hardly one voter that would be found to vote for Lord Henry Grosvenor. (Cheers.) No one had ever ventured to contradict or deny one word of what he was about to tell I them. (Cheers.) He went on an estate at Bodyke which belonged to a man earned O'Callaghau, who bought it In the year 1850. Directly he purchased the estate he raised the rents all round in order that he might raise money to pay the mortgages. The land was more or leee mountain- ous, with great boulders upon it, a lot of it being utterly unusable. It was reclaimed not by flie landlord, but by the tenant. The landlord never epent a penny upon it. lie (Mr. Waddy) was given, ie understand that the rent of one farm was originally £2O a year, but he had only got the landlord', taco;pis from 1852, when the tenant paid £25 165, In 1854 the rent was raised to £32 10e.— (" Sh!ane.")—in 1855 to £4O. in 1858 to £46—(' Shame ") —in 1864 to £49, and in 1870 to £56 Sc 61. (Renewed cries of "Mame!) And then we in England wondered that the Irish tenants grumbled. (Laughter.) They might say that that Was an exceptional case, but It was not. There was another place occupied by a widow, named Bridget Nugent 51 years of age. He bad only been able tie obtain the re-' neipts from 1871, but the woman went to the farm in 1861 as a bride. The house she and her husband lived in was a poor dilapidated structure, and he was told by her that they used on very stormy nights to go and sleep under the hedge because they were afraid of the house being blown about their ears. The landlord would do nothing, and accordingly when Mrs. Nugent came into what was thought in these parts a great fortune—the sum of £2oo—the money was in- vested in building a new house upon the site of the old one. She and her husband were at that time paying a rent of £3O a year, and they had a lease which expired, be be- lieved, in the year 1870. Suffice it to say, that directly the lease expired, because they had built this good house and because Michael Nagent had done a great deal towards re- claiming the bog, the landlord raised the rent from £3O to £B3 a year. (" Shame.") The Government valuation of that land, including the house the tenants had bailt them- selves, was only £39 a year, and yet Michael Nugent and his widow after him paid £B3 a year. ("Shame.") Michael Nugent, who was of a delicate constitution,died in 1873, and the plucky widow struggled courageously o bring up her family. It was constantly contended by the Tories that these people could pay their rents if they liked. This was utter nonsense. This poor woman had been borrowing money for years to enable her to make up her rent, and he produced 20 of the promissory notes she had given, begin- ning in 1878, and more than a score of notes from the bank for the discounts she had paid. He obtained from her those documents, and three days after he left her, the house was sold over her head, at the town of Ennis. Thus she was turned out homeless and destitute fromthe house which had been built by her own money. ("Shame.") He had got about thirty of such cases. and the difficulty with him was which to pick out. The Irish people had been telling us of these things for he did not know how long. We have ignored and passed them over, and even now the remedy was to apply more coercion. Would they as Englishmen submit to that? (" Cries of No.") Did it strike them that that was the right policy to be supported? He called noon them to do all they could to wipe away from England the shameful stain which rested upon her. (Cheers.) '[here was a great deal said about the National League governing Ireland with American dollars, but such a statement was the vilest and most ridiculous nonsense. (Hear, hear,) There was one sense in which the National League gov- erned Ireland, and it was this—that the National League was practically Ireland. (Cheers.) And if the Tory Government proposed to destroy the National League, they would want a mighty big extinguisher. (Laughter and cheers.) He did not believe there was any danger to the Union in granting Ireland dome Rule, but he did be- lieve there was danger from the &her policy. If Ireland again had her own Parliament, her people would be firm and loyal as they were when they had their own Parlia- ment, and when the British Parliament passed a vote of thanks to them for their loyalty and labours. He believed there would be just and true equality. (Hear, bear.) The union now sought was a better union than that existing. It was to be the union of the ring and not the union of the handcuff. (Loud cheers.) There was a time, he had often thought, which woe exactly a parallel to our own, as far as the lapse of centories would allow it. A young king came to the grandest throne in the world; he came to reign over the chosen people of the Almighty. A deputation waited upon him, and said, "Thy father made our yoke heovy. Do thou now relieve us from our burdens, and deal with us with fairness and evality.'"The young King had two sets of councillors, as her Molests, had now. (Laughter.) There were some that bent beneath the weight of years, and were sanctified by their conduct and experience. The King went to them. Ha (Mr. Waddy) did not koow who was the spokesman for them ; history had not handed down to us ths name of the "Grand Old Man " of that day. (Cheers.) The old man said to the King, "Deal tenderly with this people; deal fairly with them, be reason- able and just, and they will be thy servants and thy friends for ever." (Cheers.) LORD HENRY GROSVENOR'S CANDI- DATURE. MEETING AT WESTON. In support of the candidature of Lord Henry Gro4vrnor a public meeting was held in the Church schoolroom, Weston. on Monday evening. Ur. E. J. Norman, of Runcorn, occupied the chair, and there was a moderate attendance. _

The Chairman remarked that that was an Unionist meet. Mg. He thought it was very necessary to make that ex- planation, because a great many persons who did not agree upon ordinary politicil matters had sank their party names in this great crisis, and were standing shoulder to shoulder in face of what they considered a cammon danger. They had had many eminent men in the district assisting the candidature of both Mr. Brunner and Lord Grosvenor, and the only difference was tbat whereas the speakers on the other side were well paid for their services, the Unionist speakers came down to give their assistance from pure love of the work. He earnestly asked them to support Lord Grosvenor when the time came to record their votes. (Cheers.)

• M. Steele moved the following resolution :—" That in all legislation relating to Ireland we still affirm the absolute necessity for the mtintenance of the following principles : (1) The supremacy of the Imperial Parliament ; (2) the maintenance of the union; and (3) the protection of the Irish Loyalists." The Euglish Horne of Commons was the greatest legislative assembly that ever was, and they did not want to hurl it from the proud position it now occupied. EY the death of their late member they had lost a man who was perhaps the best representative that that division could possibly have, and he was sure that they would wish to have a successor worthy of him. That would be the best compliment they could pay to his memory. Lord Henry Grosvenor was a man who held the political principles of their late member, and he was sore he would follow in the footsteps of him who had been taken away from them by the hands of death. (Cheers.) Captain Barnes seconded the resolution. In the course of his speech he referred to the Glenbeigh evictions, and showed the tyranny of the Irish Nationalists in these cases. He said that the rents owing were for a period of five years, and amounted to £7,000, and the landlord agreed to take one year's rent instead of holding out for the full amount. These terms tbe tenants agreed to accept, but the National League stepped in and ordered them not to pay, and thus the landlord was bound to evict. _
_ Mr. Thomas Ford supported the resolution, which the Chairman declared carried.

The Rev. William Preston moved, and Dr. MacDougall seconded, a proposition that the meeting considered , Lord Henry Grosvenor a fit and proper person to represent them in Parliament, and pledging themselves te use all legitimate means to secure his return. Both gentlemen spoke strongly against the dark deeds done by Moon- lighters and ass.,sains in Ireland, and concluded with an earnest appeal on behalf of the candidature of Lord Henry Grosvenor. The resolution was put to the meeting and carried. A vote of thanks to the Chairman and the singing of the National Anthem brought the meeting to a close. UNIONIST MEETING AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday night a crowded meeting of the supporters of Lord Henry Grosvenor was held in Runcorn Public Hall. The proceedings were charac- terised by censiderable enthusiasm. Mr. J. Brundrit presided, and he was supported on the platform by Sir Henry Havelock Allen, M.P., Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., Mr. A. Patten, Dr. McDougall, Dr. Steele, Rev. W. Preston. Mr. A. Timmins, and a number of local gentlemen, The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said he did not consider that Lord Henry Grosvenor's youth was any objection to his candidature. (Hear, hear.) If they had a few members in Parliament who would talk less and vote in the right way, it would be more conducive to the public good. (Applause) They had met that night, Liberals and Tories, to preserve the unity of the Empire against the Seoaratist party. That party strove to gain ground in the country, and the Unionists were doing their best to prevent them, and be hoped that by a strong vote on Saturday next the electors of that division would show that they were as determined as other parts of the country to maintain the union which had been the pride of all Britons, and the envy of almost every nation in the world. (Applause.) Mr. T. W. Russell. M.P., who was received with loud cheers, said that this election was not to be fought on nar- row and personal issues ; and it was the duty of eery pitriotic cit,zm to set aside all rn:nor issues, and to fight for their country. (Applause.) After stating the cans, of the disruption in the Liberal party, he proceeded to ask what Mr. Gladstone's bills propesed to do. With regard to the Land Purchase Bill, all he would say was that if Mr. Gladstone was sent back to power that bill would have something like a glorious resurrection. Speaking on the Home Rule Bill, be referred to the clause proposing to ex- clude the Irish members from the Imperial Parliament, Mr. Brunner had said that the clause had been dropped by Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone was far too wise to give any pledge to that effect. Bat supposing the Mali members were to be allowed to remain at Westminster, what effect would they hays there? If, for instance, the question of Free Tra& came up—and they would be face to face with this question before many years were over what would be the effect of the Irish vote? They knew the Irish . . ... _ _

to be Protectionist, while the majority of Englishmen were in favour of Free Trade, but if to the minority in Parliament were added the votes of 103 Irish members, Free Trade would be abolished and Protection re-established in Eng- land. That was what Mr. Brunner would Ming about by the retention of the Irieh members in Parliament. The Irish members had told them that it was an extended scheme of local government that was •wanted for Ireland. But no system of local government would make Ireland a nation. It was delightful to hear the Irish members who in 1885 denounced Mr. Gladstone, orate in the Market-places, laughing in their sleeves all the time at the gullibility of John Bull. All this talk about local government was pure moonshine ; the Irish made a much wider demand, and in support of this statement be referred to Mr. William Redmond's speech at the Chicago convention. Proceeding to deal with the land question he said it had been stated in that divieioz that the Govern- ment were pledged to a purchase scheme. They were pledged to a purchase scheme, but they would be born fools . . . .

if, after the fate that befell Mr. Gladstone's measure, which , pledged the credit of the country, they went upon the same lines but Mr. Gladstone had himself admitted that it I could be done without taxing imperial credit, and the • Government would do it without taxing the country. When I Mr. O'Connor and Mr. Mahoney made the statement they were either deliberately misrepresenting the Government, or they did not know what they were saying. The Govern- ment's policy was to convert the occupier into the owner of the soil, and Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain bad been able to do far more for the tenant farmers of Ireland than all the Nationalists and Gladstonians could do for them The Land Hill which had been passed was not only a mea- sure of jestice but of generosity, and he believed that next session something would have to be done for the landlords in order that they might not have to bear the whole burden of the economical revolution created by the measure. Re• ferring to the evictions, details of which had bsen laid be- fore the electors at Radical meetings, he said that had the (Opposition allowed that Land Bill to pass three months ago, not one of these evictions wohld have taken place, and now that it had become law, there need never be another unjust eviction in Ireland. (Applause.) The electors of that division had a heavy responsibility placed upon them. He asked them to brush aside Mr. Brunner's per- sonal claims, and to forget Lord Henry Grosvener's youth, and to play the part of men at this great period in their country's history. (Applause.) He concluded by moving a resolution affirming the necessity of maintaining the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, of preserving the Union, and of protecting the Irish Loyalists. (Applause.) General Sir Henry Havelock-Allen. M.P,, seconded the motion, and said that while they should not decide this election upon personal qualities, the very best tribute they could pay to their late respected member would be to return in his place a man who sought their suffrages on precisely the same principles. (Applause.) He (Sir Henry) had in the past been a Radical of the Radicals, and a staunch fol- lower of ens whom he should never support again. Mr. Gladstone had made a complete and a most extroardinary turn about, right in the teeth of all his former opinions. (Applause.) He referred to Mr. (Iledstone's statements regarding the high members prior to ihe election of 1885, aud asked how it was possible for Mr. Gladstone, with a frailty far exceeding any frailty accorded to the other sex, to be the first to turn round and succumb to the political temptation, and that his moral virtue was the first to give way under the strain? Now Mr. Gladstone-professed that these men were constitutionalists, willing to gain constitu- tional ends by constitutional means. He asked this coun- try to commit the interests of the Irish loyalists to the care of people who he had declared were marching through ra- pine to the disintegration of an empire and de- sired them to believe that in the future thorwould become a sourcs of strength and of unity to this nation, which in reality they were trying to tear to pieces, When a man who had held one set of principles for nearly fifty years soddenly turned his coat, as Mr. Gladstone had, lie must have been wrong either in the past or at the present He (Sir Henry) believed be was right in the past when be. was maintaining the constitutional principles which had become a cardinal doctrine of every Liberal and Conserva- tive, and that be was fatally wrong now, when he had al- lowed his mind to be biased, his conscience to be seared, and the whole tone of his political life to be changed, by adopting the course which in earlier times he had de- precated, but which he was now unable to withstand. The difference between his (Sir Henry's) position and Mr. Brun- ner's was one of which he was justly proud, If he as a Radical had refused to follow a man because he believed he was leading to danger, he had at all events done so because he had woilred out his conscientious convictions step by step and had followed them to the end. Personally he had not one word to say against Mr. Brunner. He sat with him in Parliament for a short time. At first he recognised in John a good Radical, but he thought that towards the end of that time there was a little wavering about him which showed that he west on the principle of watching the

" Married Women's Rights and Liabilities in rela- tion to contracts, torts, and trusts" is ,the title of an important work written by Mr. Montague Lush, and published by Messrs. Stevens and Sons, London. Mr. Lush is the author of "The Law of Husband and Wife," and is therefore particularly qualified to deal with the special branch of the subject in the volume before us. The work is intended.for the guidance of legal practitioners in the diffichlt questions that so froriently arise, not only in theEigh Court, but also in the County Courts, as to the legal rights of a mar- ried woman to maintain actions, act in a trust, &c., and the liability of herself and her husband on her contraets and torts. It explains how to determine whether, a contract which she makes is to be treated as Made with respect to her separate property or as agent for her husband; what are the remedies of her creditors against her 'separate property in different cases; the rights and position of her trustee in ban. kruptcy ; and the effect of a restraint against antici- pation upon the rights of her creditors, etc. "Sea Music "is the title of the Summer Volume of the Canterbury Poets, published by Mr. Walter Scott. I is an snthology of the best poems and pas- sages descriptive of the sea, selected from the writings of Euglish poets from Shakespeare to the present day. As may well be supposed, it makes a charming book—one which cannot but form a pleas. ant companion to those who are holidaying either at the sea-side or in the country. The poems have been collected and rranged by Mrs. W. Sharp. author of "Women's Voices," "Great Musical Composers," &c. "Early English Poetry" constitutes the August issue of the Canterbury Poets. This,important work is edited by Mr. H. Macaulay Fitzgibbon, who has supplied a lengthy critical introduction which is in itself worth the shilling which is charged for the whole volume. As some of the poems go back some 500 years. and would scarcely be intelligible to the ordinary reader, if presented as they were originally written, the editor has here and there modernised the phraseology, but he has wisely made no alteration which he did not deem, absolutely necessary. There is an index of authors and titles and there is be- ssdes a large number of interesting and valuable notes. We extract from the volume" a love ditty of about the year 1,300.'- -.. b„.. " For her love I nark and care, For her love I droop and dare, sft For her love my bliss is bare, And an wax wan. For her love in sleep I slake, For her love all night I wake, For her love 1 mournise make,
_ More than any man."

"The life of Carlyle" is issued this month in the "Great Writers'' series. It is from the pen of Dr. Richard Garnett, and it is in every respect a very satisfactory performance. There has been a great deal written about Carlyle since his death, and as his failings have been magnified, there is danger of a wrongesstimatebeiug ,formed of the character of the great writer.- The tresent life of Carlyle avoids "the falsehood of extremes," and the-reader who per- uses this volume will rise from it with a feeling that Carlyle was at great a'nd good man, eiith,litiman weak- nesses, and human infirmitiec The work is made the more valuable by a eopious index, and a carefully prepared bibliography. , Defoe's ",Captain !Singleton " is putliehed in the Camelot Series. It records, to quote the original title, "the life, adventures, and piracies otthei famous Captain Singleton." There is an introduotion and notes by Mr. H. Halliday Sperling, mai a list in I chronological order of Da foe's works. It is needless ' to say that any thing from the pen of the author of Robinson Crime must be interestiog, and Captain Bingirnoa is therefore an interesting story. It shows ' that Defoe had great geographical knowledge, and knew how to put it to good use. The public are deeply indebted to Mr. Walter Scott for,issuing so many excellent works in this cheap form. The -* Westminster Review "for; August opens with a suggestive article on '‘4 John Bright and the Irish Question." It gives ample quotations from Mr. Bright's earlier speeches, which go to show that he is • now as much behind publie opinion se he was,twenty years ago,ll advance of it. We have the seeond•part of a contribution ori "Technical • Education and Foreign Competition "—a subject which can scarcely be too much discussed in these days. Other interesting articles are :—Prehistorio Surgery, Young Australia, Irish Diet and Irish Discontent, Port Hamilton, &o. The writers in the "independent section "deal with the social problem, and European aristocracy. There is the usual thoughtful review of Contemporary Literature, and Home Affairs. " Seribner's Magazine" opens with the fifth batch of the "Unpublished Letters of Thackeray," and very pleasant reading they are. They revel the great novelist as nothing else could, and they show him to be one of the most genial and loveable of men. The picturesque quality of Holland, with illustrations from drawings by the author—Mr. E. 8 Markham—is a special feature in the current issue. "A girl's life eighty years ago "is completed; it has proved choice reading. Perhaps the most important illustrated article is one by Mr. N. S. Staler on "The instability of the Atmosphere." The capital story "Seth's Brother's Wife" seems to be re whin°.° a cul- minating point; and there is a fine completed tale— " The lost Rembrandt "—by Mr. T. R. Sullivan, There are several other interesting papers, and the poetry is as ueual above the average of magazine ' verse. ' "rho English Illustratel " as a Sixpenny Maga- zine continues to be worthy of being spoken of as first-class. Mr. Hugh Thompson is funnier than ever in his illustrations of the poem "Sir Dilberry Diddle." The second part is given of "Walks in the Wheat- fields" (illustrated) ; and another capital article, capitally illustrated, is "A Visit. to• the Dutch country-house," by May (7rommelin. Mr. J. E. Hodgson, R.A., Professor of Painting in the Royal Academy, is the author of a bulky pamph- let with the title of " Fifty Years of British Art, as illustrated by the pictures and drawings in the Man- chester Royal Jubilee Exhibition." Professor Hodg- son speaks, of course, as one having authority, and it is gratifying to see that, as a critic, he is more anxious to point to beauties than rail at defects. The reader who wants to thoroughly understand the die - tinctive features of British art cannot do better than rely on him as guide, philosopher, and friend. The work Is published by Mr. John Heywood, Man - chester. "Reasons why the English Committee's Report on Pasteurism does not settle the question," is the title of a well-reasoned pamphlet by Mr. Ben. Bryan. The reasons are vigorously stated, and they certainly warrant the conclusion that the question is by no means settled.

"Income Tax—bow to get it Refunded" is the title of a useful little hand-book by Mr. Alfred Chapman. The fact that it has reached a fourth edition is evi- dence of its having hit the mark. There are many people who sn'unit to an unjust assessment because they do not know the right way to the remedy. The work in question is exactly what they require. The directions given are plain and practical; and they cover every possible case. The shilling spent in the book may save many a pound. It is published by Messrs. E. Wilson & Co., London.

heir to the earlship of IVith aM Retort, fourteenth in the Roll of Scotland. .Tien prouder heritage was that of Thane of Len,: nox, which dates back to the time of the Con- quest, on evidence much more assured than that of Lordßrassey's great forbear " the Lorddeßresci." He would also, had he lived, have inher;ted the title of Hereditary Steward of Strathearn,which dates back to 1473. But he preferred " Mrs. or Miss," and has lived with her through thirty-one years of hard- ship and penury. The peerages are all very reticent on the fortunes of Lord Drummond, Debrett inge- niously recording his residence as "Brooklands, near New York, U.S.A." Brooklands has a fine territorial sound, by no means suggesting the apartments of a railway gatekeeper. As Lord Drummond leaves a daughter, who, if the marriage was legal, is heiress to the estates of the Earldom, a cause celebre, turning upon the old question of "Mrs. or Miss," may shortly come before our courts of law. The season that is slowly flickering to its end has at least been marked by one important secial revo- lution. There were great complaints last year of the way young married women had taken the places of girls, so that in every ball room the beauties in their first season could find no partners, while pretty young married women had their programmes full from the moment they entered the ball room. All this was very bad. It is very bad still. But this year matters seemed to be even going worse. Young men would crowd in just before supper time, hang about the door ways, and not dance at all. There was the same complaint wherever you went. The explanation was curious. The fat young men found dancing fatiguing. If they &- gen they should go on—and so they did not begin. And the reason of the fatigue was the number of round dances. Waltz succeeded waltz. All the old square dances were left out. A few years ago a ball room beauty would ask as to a partner about to be introduced, "Is he a round or a squa,•e? " But that was a few years ago. Now Ithey should all be "rounds." They took their own I revenge, concentrated their attention on the sup- per and did not dance at all. The question got to be very serious as it affected the marriage market. Near the end of this season the quadrille re-appeared. There were pauses in the fury of round dancing, and the coated animal deigned to take his place. Next year we shall have plenty of lancers and quadrilles.

L Al' 14,' ST NEWS . __ At Malta aed Sicily the deaths conseqaent upon the epidemic of cholera are daily increasing. In Naples the disease is stagnant. John Hammond, of Old Elvet, Durham, for trial at the sessions on the charge of stealing a gold watch and chain. The drought is causing a great deal of anxiety in East Lancashire. The Rishton reservoir is entirely empty. The canal traffic has been stopped for went of water, and such a drought has not been known for 60 years.
