CAPTURE OF A SLAVER.—DESPE. FIGHT. Friday night's" Gazette" contains a despatch from the senior naval officer at Zanzibar recording the gallant cap- tore of a slave dhow. at Pemba, and consequent release of 53 slaves by Lieutenant Fegen, of H.M.S. Turquoise. The lieutesant and his men behaved with the greatest bravery, receiving severe wounds in the fight. Eleven Arabs were killed, and one English sailor has since died of his wounds. It appears that of thirteen Arabs on board nine were the most notorious slave dealers in Pemba. In all there were twenty men armed with snider rifles and swords, Captain Woodward says cannot speak too highly of the brave and gallant behaviour of Lieut. Pegan and b.is crew. He then enumerated the disadvantages under which the pinnace was placed, and appeals to the Admiralty for recognition of the gallantry of his subordinates. This recommendation has been acted upon. Fegan being pro. moted to the rank of commander, and promotions having been granted to six seamen and a soldier of marines.

twenty-third clauseothigh pliminished the value of the bill to Irish tenints by °vibelf.' The clause originall7 gave full discretion to the Irish. Land Commissioners as to the re-adjustment of rents; but the amendment of Lord Cado- gan had bound them down to an iron rule which destroyed the value of the bill to such an ex' ent that it mattered little to the Irish tenants whether the bill was postponed for another year, and he washed his hands of all responsibility on the subject. He asked the Government to give informa- tion on one of two things—were they going to adhere to the , amendment of Lord Cadogan, or weuld they postpone the consideration of the Lords' amendments until they could he I fully considered by those interested in the bill 2—Mr. A. 1 BALFOUR insisted that the amendment in no sense li altered the substance of the clause. All it did was to put in clear and unmisttkeable lan- guage what would be the natural operation of the Intense, and at the proper time be should be prepared to justify it. He did not think that hon. members would be prepared to take upon themselves the responsibility of des- troying the bill which extended to Irish tenants such sub• utantial benefits.—Sir W. HARCOURT ridiculed the asser- tions of the Chief Secretary for Ireland, and insisted that the amendment was not simply an explanation. It was more than that—it was an alteration that made vital and fundamental alterations in the bill, and to such extent that It rendered the measure worthless. He accused the Govern- ment of stabbing their own measures in the back in the House of Lords.—Mr. W. SMITH denied that they bad agreed to the amendment to buy the votes of Uls. er, and accused Sir W. . THE CONDITION OP BATTERSBY-LANE. Sir,—Would you kindly allow me space in your next is- sue to draw the attention of the authorities to the state of the above lane, owing to the refuse of the town being carted up here, instead of to Longford to burn it oat of the way. Instead of so doing, we are pestered with the wind blcwing it all about the neighbourhood. I would also ask our trades- people to be careful about their business correspondence being committed to the waste paper basket to be carted up here by the dust carts, and thus be exposed. Again, as winter is approaching, may I ask if we cannot be favoured with a little better light (a Bray's lamp) under the railway bridge and at the entry sod near the bridge. It is really very unpleasant for males or females at present, to say nothing of darker nights.—Yours,

we should like. Let your readers peruse the reports daily published, of the inquiry now going on in Wales respect- ing the recent tithe riots. They will dad that the Ecclesi- astical Cominissioners are at their wits end what to do with their farms The fact is English farmers are, coward like, taking one of the courses suggested by Lord Salisbury —"pay or quit." Why should they I' Rent or no rent we want the land farming, and it is time this emigration panic , was stopped. I see the " &and trd " states that it is pos- sible to stand at one point, about 30 miles from London, and count 75 farms all without tenants, and this in a county —Essex—that used to rank as one of the first in agricul- ture. We have had none of the heartrending eviction scenes, but one can fancy the tag there has been at the heart strings in many an Englieh home ere emigration has been thought of, or, ere a removal from the quiet coun- try side to the worry and noise of a busy town, was re- sorted to.

Lord Salisbury most be in a sad and pitiable position jnst now. History has no record of a Prime Minister boast- ing sach high and spirited principles as his lordship, hay- ing to swallow those principles. tie has only himself to blame; did he not compare Mr. Goschen and Lord Hart- ington to an Egyptian skeleton and Rip Van Winkle, and fancied them in their inner councils with Lord Derby steadily pouring cold water upon both? Well, he has them, and

"If I'd MY way I bed rather We should go ti w k an' part They take one way, we take Cother— Guess it wouldn't break my heart." It would have the good effect of bringing the Tory party more in accordance with 19th century ideas, and relieve them of the odious position in which so many Tories con- fess to their shame they are in. Since Mr. Ashrnead Bartlett, in the Public Hall, de- nounced Mr. Jesse Collings and Mr. Chamberlain as dema- gogues. not quite two years since, the people have learned something, of which not the least is that the Tories may, in the place of political talent, have the not-to-be-despieed power of reckoning men up, and it will take a deal to get "poor Joe" and Jesse into harness with Mr. Howorth fol- lowing submissively. The Tories have had enough of the Unionists and from all sides we hear most fearful denuncia- tions of the rotten "crutch." But while these wrongly-called Unionists are steeped to the eyes in trouble, what of Ireland? Wh A. has led to her present troubles? Fronde, the historian, tells us" English in Ireland "(vol. ii, p 23)—"The landlords of Ireland cared ,no more for the souls and bodies of those who were commit- ted to their charge than the driver of a West Indian planta- _lion for the herds of slaves whose backs were blistering in the cane fields." As John Mitchell said :—" The Irish land- lord was a sponge filled in Ireland to be squeezed in Eng- land." To quote again from Mr. Froude—" The Russian government has been called despotism tempered with assass- ination. In Ireland landlordism is tempered by assassina- tion. The landlords were for the most part aliens in bleed and religion. They represented conquest and confiscation, and they had gone on from generation to generation wath an indifference to the welfare of the people which would not have been tolerated IR England or Scot- land." Another of these paper Unionists, John Bright, speaking in Dublin, said—" Ireland is a country from which thousands have been driven by the will of the land- owner, and the power of the law. The great evil of Ireland is thie, that the Irish peeple—the Irian nation—are dis- possessed from the soil, and what we ought to do is to pro- vide for and to aid in their restoration to it by all measures of justice." These two, Mr. Fronde and Mr. J. Bright, are now standing side by side with the most autocratic landlord Europe has in it. CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: SUFFERER.
div.p: A SUFFERER.

LEGAL OR ILLEGAL? 81r,—There is one mystery about the Warrington Free Library which many peeple would like to see cleared up, and that is, whether it is being carried on legally or ille- gally. It has been pretty plainly asserted several times, and I see vol make a point of it in your leading columns last week, that the local authorities are breaking the law in charging a subscription at a library which is mainly sup- ported by a penny rate. It is amazing to me that this matter has not been settled one way or another before now. I know that a large amount of public interest is taken in the question, and some are rather inclined to think that the authorities are acting quite within their powers,while not a few are pretty nearly convinced of the contrary. But every one's opinion is, so to speak, more or less in a state of suspension on the subject. It seems to me that the matter might be very easily cleared up. Let a member of the Town Council, at its next meeting, ask the Town Clerk, who is expected to keep the council in the legal pith, to state dis- tinctly whether or not in his opinion the library is being conducted legally. The point, ac I understand it, is whether the law makes any provision for privileges, such as taking a book home, on account of a subscription. I have no doubt that Mr. Brook will be quite prepared to give an answer one way or another and also to give reasons for his answer. I can assure the member of the Council who un- dertakes to do what I have suggested, that he will afford sat- ' Isfactton to not a few of his constituents.-1 am, sir, A RATEPAYER.
Warrington, Magnet 10th, 1887.

THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. Sir,—You will perhaps allow me to again say a few words on the subject of the intercepting depots, as I see it was referred so at the last meeting of the Town Council. The remark I wish to make is that thou who are mering such an outcry about the depots seem to have a very plentiful lack of local patriotism. Here we have a scheme put in opera- tion, and it is admitted by everybody that if it can be car- ried out it will be not merely of the greatest utility to Warrington, but a distinct and important advance in the practical application ef sanitaty science. It has, we may say, been barely put into operation. and thc e who are responsible for its working have bad scarcely any opportu- nity of gathering those lessons which in the management of a Lew thing can only be had by experience, when it has been pat ,o a test by the remarkable and long-continued heat of the weather such as it will probably not have to again undergo for a generation to come. I think this last statement may be reasonably made as I the ether day saw it had been asserted by a high made, official, who has to de with the sanitary work of the country, that such a drought as we have had this summer had not been known before in the memory of man. Yet no sooner have the sen- sitive snardling apparatus of a few gentlemen—not many. I believe—been affected by a few odours from the depOts under the very extraordinary test through which they have been put, than they begin to cry out that the scheme is a failure and threaten or hint at all sorts of pains and penal- ties if it is not snuffed out at once. Considering that the successful working of this scheme would be a world-wide credit to Warrington, and that bringing it prematurely to an end weuld be a great loss to the town I think it may fairly be said that we would have thought more of their meat patriotism if they had not taken up their cry in such ill-censidered haste.—Yours, S. M.

THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION. Sir,—ln a late issue of the "Examiner," I noticed two 1 letters on the above mentioned matter—one signed "William Roberto" and the other "J. J. Longbow." I think I am competent to speak as to London, after something like 20 years experience in every part; and without reading Mr. Langhom's remarks that he had laboured in a "fashionable Wept End ,parish," I should have known it, because he says public-houses are more plentiful in the poor than in the rich quarters. It is quite plain Mr. Longhorn "stuck " in the West End, and didn't trouble to look in the East, and that his map was one of those bogus affairs, got up to encourage a Local Option craze. I know or no wealthier parts of London than the City, the Strand, and Oxford-street; and I am perfectly certain public-houses are more often met with there, in proportion to space, than any where else. I can't believe Mr. Long- horn ivquite so foolish as he looks when he says that wealthy brewers "plant their public-houses where they will do the meet prosperous trade, namely, in the haunts of poverty." The paradox that poverty makes the brewers rich, and that the brewers do the moet prosperous trade where there is no money—l mean where poverty prevails— is too abstruse for me. I own I am beaten here but thank Providence, another " Cocker" or" Coleus° " has come to light—" J. J. ',lngham," As for that letter of "William Roberts," it is so exces- sively "tall" that I scarcely like to tackle it. "is he a giant that writes thusly ?" Can't a writer be sincere be- cause he writes anonymeuely? and need his sincerity be doubted (aide W. Roberts' letter) for the same reason? I once heard a gentleman say, pointing triumphantly to this same "William Roberts," "There goes a man who never tasted intoxicatieg liquor in his life !" Need I say, I very much doubted that ; not' because it is too absurd to believe, but because Mr. Roberts spoke, and always does speak, with such an immense assumption of knowledge on 'drink.'' We, who don't believe in " Local Option," (I suppose this title is always dropt now because it doesn't " go down," except with ndders and Fanatics) shall not grieve because Mr. Roberts "cannot consent" to discuss with anonymous writers the temperance cause. We can afford to loso even his " awf al light and leading," conscious that we are working strictly on the lines ef Scripture, which says that "all things were given for ern use, and not abuse." And it is sheer impertinence for a set of sham philanthropists to try to dictate what we shall drink. We are individually responsible for our actions, at least my spiritual pastor often told me so; and I believe him. Lie need not be specially wise who says drunkenness is a curse, and if these said teetotallers would teach temperance in all things, and let Local Option, or absolute prohibition, or anxiety to meddle in individual rights, go to the proper plaoe for shooting such rubbish, they would have no more earnest supporter than yours truly,
UNCLE TO BY. don't Sign my proper name ; it looks (to me) too bumptious and immodest.

THE PARTY IN PLACE. Sir,—Things seem to be going very bad just now for the Party in place. They have been too sanguine, and have quite ignored the fact that the English people when they once set fairly to work to consider cause and effect rarely make a mistake. The Tories fancied they were all Tight when they had get bold of two or ti ree prominent Liberals. Crutch or no crutch, they intended to keep in office if bespattering Joseph and his brethren with fulsome praise would do it. From Spalding to Bridgeton it has been one continued series of eye-openers for the Separatists. The people see clearly that only the Gladstone programme can bind and give solidity to the empire. Justice to Ireland is recognised as the first thing to be attended to. If we claim to be a thoughtful nation, it could not be otherwise, seeing what we do every day at home. Is it not clear that with all our privileges we in England And it impossible to get along as

div.head: )liR LONI)6N LETTER.
div.p: )liR LONI)6N LETTER.

LONDON. TITURSDAX. Matters in the House of Commons are proceeding very quietly, not to say with intolerable dulness. There still loom ahead one or two debates which should be of prime importance. The Lords have yet to deal with the Irish Land Bill, and they are suspected of intent so to maul it that a contest may arise with the House of Commons. There is a final fight to be raised over Sir Henry Wolff's Egyptian pie-rile, upon the question of providing for his salary .• and there is the state of things that would be created supposing the Government were to proclaim the Land League under the latest Crimes Act. But the stars in their courses are fighting for the Government. It is impossible to get up a momentous row in a small House. Every day the attendance is thinned, for though the Con- servative whips steadfastly set their faces against making provision for pairs, pairs are individually picked up, and where any difficulty arises, even loyal Conservative members are able to invent reasons of personal moment sufficient to carry them off. Thus questions which, touched in the high tide of Parliamentary attendance, might be counted upon to have momentous consequences, shrivel into insignificance when dealt with before half empty benches. But taken individually none of the three ques- tions alluded to is likely to prove a serious obstacle in the way of the adjournment. The Lords will surely be too wise at this time of day to refuse con- firmation to the Land Bill. It is not a Conserva- tive measure, being on the whole conceived in the interest of the tenants. But it is a sop solemnly pledged to the Dissentient Liberals, designed to soothe their disturbed consciences, and enable them to continue their support of a Tory Government. If it be rejected by the Lords, Mr. Chamberlain will be placed in a position, the weight of which he is not the man to bear all to his own hurt. The farce of Sir Henry Wolfrs mission to Egypt is played out, and as the bill of costs cannot be honourably disowned, it will be paid after a due amount of grumbling. The Irish question is, as usual, the most difficult. Lord Salisbury's speech at the Man- sion House last night seemed to imply fixed inten- tion of proclaiming the National League. This can be done only when Parliament is sitting, and its announcement will doubtless be put off to the latest possible moment. This will limit the opportunities for retaliatory obstruction, perhaps, not without ensuring the secret satisfaction of Mr. Parnell. The cause of Ireland and its champions is steadily making way in the estimation of the English voter, and this is too precious a gain to be imperilled by a free fight in the House of Com- mons. Parliament may, therefore, after all, be pro- prorogued before the boundary of September is crossed. The death of Lord de Ramsey will add another to the curiously frequent opportunities of testing the drift of public opinion at the present crisis. The sitting member for North Huntingdonshire, con- sequent upon the death of his father, takes his place in the House of Lords, and there is a vacancy I in the division. North Huntingdonshire, on the face of it, judged by the fact that it was not con- tested at the last General Election, has come to be regarded as a Tory stronghold. This is not the case, for at the preceding General Election Lord E. Stewart-Gordon contested the division and was beaten only by 365 votes. In the coming contest, the Liberals mean to correct that. I believe that at one time Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice, who has now re- turned to the Liberal fold, was talked of in connec- tion with the constituency, Lord Edmond Fitz- maurice has considerable family influence in the county. and was regarded as a very hopeful candi- date. But another, still more generally acceptable in the locality has come to the front, and vill, it is confidently hoped, carry the Liberal flag to the top of the pole. In the meantime political attention is concentrated upon Northwich. This is a much bolder endeavour than North Huntingdonshire. Here a Tory majority of over 450 has to be trans- formed into a Liberal majority. This is essentially a contest on the question of the day, whether the tide truly has turned for Mr. Gladstone. Northwich was won at the last General Election not by a pro- fessed Conservative but by one calling himself a Liberal Unionist. As he routed the then sitting Liberal member, there is no doubt the seat was lost through Liberal voters playing the Conservative game. If they now show that they have come to their senses it will be all up with the Government and their strange a.lies. A very painful feeling has been created in the House of Commons by a statement which appears. in some of the morning papers. It is to the effect that a committee of ladies living in the neighbour- hood of Glasgow had in celebration of the Jubilee subscribed money: sufficient to en- dow a number of beds in the Dunoon Con- valescent Home, where poor women are received and cared for. Full ot loyalty, they wrote to the Queen asking permission to grace these beds with her name. 'The Victoria Beds these kind ladies thought it would be nice, to call their additions to the institution. They have received a reply in curt official language to the effect, it is stated, that the Queen disapproved of the money being devoted to the purpose assigned to it instead of being sent to the Imperial Institute. Comment on this affair is restrained by the conviction that it is incredible. It is impossible not to believe that, even if the Queen were capable of such thoughts, she would be careful not to insure publicity for a scolding to 'well-meaning ladies anxious to associate her name with a kindly act, specifically basing it on the ground that the money ought to have been sent to the Imperial Institute. A disclaimer has been anxiously looked for, and this morning, there ap- pears one of a kind from Sir Henry Ponsonby. But it is so halting and indistinct that it is necessary to await further explanations, which I firmly believe will be forthcoming. Another item in the talk of the day when the Queen's name comes in has reference to the curious silence which broods over the destination of the £70,000 which remains of the Women's Jubilee offering after provision has been made for the Prince Consort's statue. It was fully expected that the ladies who went by invitation to Windsor Castle to present the colossal purse would be hon- oured by being made the Queen's confidantes on this interesting point. But the matter was not touched upon. What with this disappointment and the unexpected satisfaction of having to pay for their tea, the ladies came away with the exuber- ance of their loyalty considerably damped. Several weeks have passed since then, and still no sign has , been made. Contrasting this with the promptness I with which as soon as the scheme was fairly set on foot and promised to be a success, decision was taken as to the devotion of the first fruits to the erection of another statue of the Prince Consort, the tardiness in dealing with the balance is much remarked upon. There are two versions of the story of Lord Drum- mond whose death, just reported from New York, has revived a long-forgotten romance of the peer- age. On the one hand, it is stated, that the woman whom he, whilst yet a boy, married, was already a wife, the other speaking of her as "Miss Eliza Har- ris." In either case it is not disputed that she was in domestic service with the lordliiag's family. Nor are subsequent events in this remarkable career dis- puted. It is agreed that the boy and' his not im- mature bride sailed straight way for America, pro- ceeding thither as steerage passenge.rs, and that he worked as a day labourer in the neighbourhood of the docks in New York, passing onward to the post of packer in a wholesale clothing house, acting as gateman on the elevated railway, finally becoming clerk in a clothing manufactory, whence he drifted into the position of a confirmed and starving in- valid. NORTHWIOH ELECTION. (Continued from Page 6.) The division has been most vigorously canvassed, amongst the most ardent workers in addition to the candidates being Mrs. and Mis"s Brunner, and Lady Henry GrosVenor. The poll commences at eight o'clock this (Saturday) morning, and will close at eight in the evening. Having been sealed up, the ballot boxes will be taken by the presiding officers to the Northwich Police Station, where they will be given into the custody of the High Sheriff (Mr. James Tomkinson), and remain there until Monday morning, when the casting up of the votes will take place at the Drill Hall. The result may be expected about noon. UNIONIST MEETING AT RUNCORN. On Thursday night a public meeting in support of the candidature of Lord Henry Grosvenor was held in Runcorn Public Hall. The body of the building was fairly well filled. Mr S Pope occupied the e.hair, and he was supported by Mr Cameron Corbett, M.P., Captain Barnes, Mr Robert Martin, M A Patten, Dr McDougall, Messrs E Barnes. Towns, Harrison, J Knowles F Joule, J Barton, F J Norman, &c. The Chairman said he had been asked to take the chair in order to show which side he was on It was well-known that he was a Liberal, and he took pleasure in following the flower of the Liberal party. (Cheers.) The Liberals and the Unionists had each their way of promoting the peace and contentment in Ireland, and union between Ireland and the United Kingdom, and the Unionists contended that theirs was the better way. They wanted both sides of the question to be heard. On the previous evening when the Unionists held a meeting in that hall, the Gladstonian Liberals in Runcorn. for fear that the raak and file of the party should hear Mr. Russell, of whom they were very much afraid, called an open-air meet- ing to keep them away. That was not a vary great compli- ment to the intelligence of their own followers. (Hear, hear.) So that they could not steal a march on the Union- ist party that night, that meeting was called at short notice. Referring to the two candidates, the Chairman said he was not going to apologise for Lord Henry Grosvenor being a young man. When Mr. Gladstone's eldest son contested Chester against Mr. Raikes, Mr. Gladstoue said youth was an advantage, because if a young man had chosen politics for a profession, he would want training, and he had better Start young than old. Don't let them argue against Lord Henry because his family had become ennobled, and don't let them say a word against Mr. Branner, whom he had worked for in other elections. With regard to Home Rale, if the Irish obtained a separate legislature they would not be allowed to deal with the land question which it was said was at the root of all the discontent and disaffection. At present the Conservative Government with the help of the Liberal Unionists could get legislation put forward—could get passed some good laws for Great Britain and Ireland. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Cameron Corbett, M.P. for a Glasgow division, said If M. Gladstone had proposed a Home Rule Bill for Scot- land similar to that proposed for the Irish people, Scotland would have been in rebellion in a month. The Irish people however, through their constitritionelly elected representa- tives declared themselves ready to accept the measure. And why ? The reason was given by the "Irish World," the organ of the Irish party in America, which said—" If we were asking for dismemberment of the British emp're I could not desire anything better than Mr. Gladstone's bill. It contrives to take away from Irishmen every inducement to wish the empire well and lays a financial foundati n for endless and embittered international controversies." It was just because the Irish party in England were asking for the I dismemberment of the empire that they desired nothing I better than the bill Mr. Gladstone provided. (Applause.) Mr. Bruener voted in favour of that bill. With re- gard to Mr. Gladstone's concessions they were made with the important consideration that they would satisfy the Irish people, and concessions which were so weighted were abso- lutely worthless to the Liberal Unionist, because it simply meant that Mr. Gladstone would make any concessions the Unionists liked if Mr. Parnell would ba kind enough to con- sent. (Applause.) Trusting Mr. Gladstone meant to trust Mr. Parnell and his fo.lowers who derived their support , from the dynamitards in America. (Applause.) In Con- clusion he urged the electors to vote for Lord Grosvenor and protect their Protestant minority from men whom Mr. Gladstone found it necessary to imprison as sources of crime. Mr. Robert Martin read extracts from the speeches of Irish members to show that their object was nothing more nor less than separation, and not to obtain measures for the amelioration of the people. He also gave his experience of boycotting in Ireland, and moped a resolution in favour of the maintenance of the Union. Mr. Richard Steele seconded the resolution which was carried. Captain Barnes moved a resolution pledging the meeting to support the candidature of Lord Grosvenor. I Mr. A. Patten seconded the resolution, which was adopted, and the meeting concluded. LORD GROSVENOR AT RUNCORN LAST NIGHT. A meeting of the supporters of the Unionist can- didate, Lord Henry Grosvenor, was held last evening in Runcorn Public Rail. There was not a very large attendance. The chair was occupied by Dr Steele, and there were also on the platform, amongst others, Mr Long, M.P., Mr Wodehouse, M.P. (Bath), the candidate, and Lady Henry Grosvenor. After the Chairman had made a brief speed], Mr. Lightburn read letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. Charles Wigg, Lady Brook (on behalf of Sir Richard Brook), and Mr. William Arthur, ex-president of the Wesleyan Conference. The latter gentleman, in the Coarse of a rather lengthy communication, said that were he an elector of Northwich Division he should certainly give his vote to Lord Henry Grosvenor. Lord Grosvenor, who had a good reception, then addressed the meeting, and said that he had been attacked by his op- ponents both on the platform and in placards. His rela- tives had also been grossly slandered. He had not replied to this abuse, because he told them at the outset that he should take no notice of personalities. (Hear, hear.) He thought that abuse and attacks of this sort were only weak weapons that had been used on behalf of a cause that was fallen. (Cheers.) That day a letter from Mr. Gladstone had appeared. It was supposed to come upon them as a surprise, but they knew it was coming, and were ready for it. In it Mr. Gladstone said that it was evident from what he was told that he (Lord Grosvenor) did not know what he was talking about when he said that the Crime.' Act was one for the suppression of crime and for the punishment of criminals, and when he also said that the Coercion Act of 1882 was far severer than the present one. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH PAR- LIAMENTARY DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. GENTLEMEN.—The death of your late member is peculiarly sad. He has been struck down at the crowning point of an honourable career, and at a moment when his neighbours. without distincti.m of class, creed, or party, were preparing to receive at his hands a noble gift, and arranging together how best to do him honour. It is with a sad pleasure that! recall how, in the precincts of the House of Commons, but a few short days ago. I held a long and friendly conference with him concerting measures for the future benefit of this distriet, in which we had both so large and deepen Merest, and how cordial was the grip of his hand at parting. Mr. VERDIN'S sad death imposes upon you the duty of electing a successor in the honourable position of member for this division. Chosen a third time by the freely elected Liberal Assoela- tiou, I ask again for a renewal of the trust you bestowed upon me twenty months ago, when over 5,000 men recorded their votes in my favour. At that time I had openly declared to you my opinion that lrelaud ought to have full power to deal with all affairs purely Irish, but that! would be no party to any enactment which would make the two millions of Irish people living in Great Britain foreigners amongst us." As your representative in the House ot Commons I rec. ,rded my vote in favour of the principle of the great measure for the better government of Ireland laid before the Howe by Mr. Gladstone—that principle being declared by Mr. Gladstone to be the establishment of a legislative assembly for Ireland em- powered to deal with purely Irish affairs. Twelve moaths ago, deceives by the promises of the Tory party and their allies, to govern Ireland by the same laws as Great Britain, deceived by the false statement that the Liberal party proposed the dismemberment of the Empire, you re- jected my offer of service. Those promises have been shamelessly broken. The Tory party and their supporters, the Dissentient Liberals, have forced upon the House of Commons and upon unwilling but helpless Ireland, a Condon Act of fearful severity, and utterly opposed to the spirit of the British Con- stitution. I ask you to punish this breast) of faith, and this you can most effectually do by pl,cing me again at the head of the poll a few days hence. I am strongly opposed. sal was last year, to the exclusion of the representatives of Ireand from the Imperial Parliament and I am still, as I was then, a firm supporter of the unity of the Empire. I will do all in my power to strengthen it' and will resist with all my might any proposal tending to weaken it. I cordially welcome Mr. Gladstone's assurance that any future measure for the purchase of Irish land for the benefit of the tenants shall involve no tisk of charge upon the British taxpayer. I rejoice greatly that the honest and kindly eff.rt made by the Liberal Leaders at the Round Table Conference has brought about a cordial agreement between them and Sir George Tre- velyan. All trueLlberals will desire that the plan for the better ;covert ment of Ireland resulting from that agreement Shall at an early date be fully and fairly placed before tha coun- try by a Government in which that true, plucky and con- filstent Liberal statesznen will sit side by side with Mr. Glad- ! ' stone. To every man who votes for me at this elm;fon will be due a large share in the honour of bringing about that happy end. My opponent comes before you as a supporter of the Tory Government, and therefore as an upholder of exceptional coercive legislation for Ireland, as a supporter of the party of privilege and excluaon, and necessarily. even in spite of him- self ,an opponent of the party of progress and freedom. I ask your 'support as a convinced Liberal. Faggot votes must be abolished, and the principle of one man, one vote" established. The present system of registratio.l results in wholesale dis- franchisement, as witness the case of Wesleyan and Primitive Methodist ministers, and it must speedily be reformed. If to-morrow any man in this Division becomes a househelder, he will not be entitled to be put on the Register until Septem- ber, 1889, and wilt not be able to vote until the let day of January 1890. Having seen mush of the benefits of the policy cf trust in the people in the matter of the control of the Liquor Trade, I am more than ever convinced of the wisdom of that policy. Finally, gentlemen, I ask for your votes as a supporter of the great Leader of the Liberal Party, Mr Gladstohe, sinePrely believing him as Ido to be a generous, a wise, and a patriotic statesman. I remain, gentlemen, Your faithful servant. JOHN T. BRUNNER. Wilmington Old Hall, Northwich, July 30th, 1887.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH DIVISION IN THE COUNTY OF CHESTER. GENTLISMEN,—By the sad removal from our midst of your late friend and Member, Mr. ROBERT VERDIN. the (muse ef the Union and of Order in Parliament has sustained a less rot to be easily replaced. Proud as I should be to devote myself to yubiic work, as a representative of my native county, the knowledge of this loss, which you more particularly must feel, incratses the sense of responsibility with which I have entered upon this present contest. The manimeus request which has reached me from the Conservative and Liberal Unionist All•ociations could alone en courage me to come forward to represent the well considered principles of p Utica prog,ess whieh your late Member stead- fastly maintained. I am prepared to support such equitable legislation as may tend tr remove the grievances of the Irish tenant farmers settle the agrarian difficulties of Ireland, and improve the per- manent relations between that country and Great Britain But I am determined on all occasions, and at any cost, to do my utmost to preserve the Unity of the United Kingdom, under One supreme Parliament. I will uphold the authority of the Executive Government. wbih is responsible for its actions to the representatives of the People in Parliament. and I will in- sist on that regard for the observance of the law, which is the surest guarantee of prosperity under the democratic institu- tions which we possess. The genuine progre3sive policy of the present Unionist Gov- ernment, as hown in their proposals for relieving the Irish tenants, for reforming the English Land Laws, for abolishing the law of primogeniture, f ir providing the labouring classes with allotments, for promoting education, readjusting taxa- tion, and establishing Local Government on an effectiNe and popu'ar basis, is before the country, and in spite of unprece- dented obstruction in Parliament, over which the firmness of tr e Government has ultimately prevailed, much of it has been advanced towards completion. Such measures convince me that from the Unionist Goverment we may confidently anti- cipate at an early date all the necessary reforms wh,ch com- mend themselves to the, country, without the risk of encoun- tering the unknown dangers and the certain delays which are involved in the 'accepts nee of the undefined Irish policy of Mr. Gladstone In particular I deere td ard to the best of my ability any measures whereby the agricultural distress now unfortunately prevailing in this county may be leiteved, and to encourage, especially by the promotion of technical education, the de- velopment of the great and special industries associated with this Division. I shall be glad to support a measure whereby marriages may be ealenanised in Noriconformir, places of worship with- out the necessi, y for the presence cf the Registrar. Any other just mearn, res which o mmand your sympathy will at all times receive my best arid most earnest consideration. lam, Gentlemen, Your most obedient Servant, HENRY GROSVENOR. Eaton Hail. Chester, August Ist, 1887.

A couple of country masons were laying a hearthstone in a new house and it being dusk before they had it laid, they could not see the spirit-level. The foreman placed the spirit-level on the hearthstone, and then lifting it gently he carried it to the door, and looking at it, said to his assistant "Man. Danny, that's it jist till a hairsbreadth." A KIND OF CREEPING SENSATION.—First coloured citizen—" Come ovah yur, Jim." Second coloured citi- zen—" Whaffur ?" " Got suthin' good." " What is it ?" " Pollynaris watah." "Pooh, watah !" "'S good, though." " Wha's taste like?" "Like yer foo,fs asleep." Tan Coaoun LINE AGAIN.—" Well, this is the tightest drawing of the colour line I ever heard of," observed Squildig, glancing up from the paper. "What is it ?" asked Mc.Swilligen. "A coloured candidate for office in Chesterfield Co., Va., was defeated because he wore a white shirt." ONE THING SHE HAD NOT GOT.—"No," snappishly said the summer boarding-house keeper to Mrs. Culture, 'bf Boston, who was inquiring as to the healthfulness of Ile locality, "No, we ain't got no typhoid germs, and 'there hain't been no calls for 'em either. Folks is want- ing everything nowadays, and ain't satisfied with clean beds and plenty of what's good to eat." SHE DIDN'T WAlT.—Child (to visitor)—" Mamma has gone to put on another dress. Visitor—" Ala?' Child— " Yes ; saw you comin' an' rua upstairs." Visitor— " Ah, hah !" Child—" Said: There comes that hateful Mrs. Anson; I wish she would stay away.' Oh, don't be in a hurry; wait till mamma comes down." AT THE REVlVAL.—Preacher—" Young men should never go to any place where they would not take their sisters. Is there a Christian young man in the audience who thinks lie may safely break this wise rule ?'' Young man under the gallery stands up. Preacher—" And what is the place, my young friend, which you think yourself justified in visiting, and yet to which you would not think of taking your sister?' Young man—'• The barber-shop, sir." SHE WAS AFRAID SHE WOULD HAVE TO KEEP A GIRL, —When Jacob Schaelkopf, the millionaire tanner of Buf- falo, took his wife around to look at a hundred- tfiousand-pounds residence which he bought recently, her only criticism—according to an American paper— was that she was afraid if she lived there she would have "to keep a girl." Husband; "You know that pretty Mrs. F. ? ' Wife: "For goodness sake, John, don't talk about 'that pretty Mrs. F.'! I can't go anywhere without hearing her praises gounded, until I am sick to deathof the sound of her name." Husband: "I was only going to tell you of a rumour I heard about her to-day." Wife: "A rumour? Oh, John, tell me all about it—that's a good soul !" It is related that a gentleman whs was trying a horse in company with a jockey noticed, after having driven him a mile or two, that he pulled pretty hard, requiring constant watching and a steady ' rein and the gentleman inquired, "Do you think it is just the horse for a lady to drive ?" "Well, sir," answered the jockey, "I must say that I shouldn't want to marry the woman who could drive that horse." A Yankee walked into a Massachusetts court one day, and spent some time in watching the proceedings. By- and-by a man was brought up for contempt of court and fined; whereupon the stranger rose and said; "How much was the fine?" "Five dollars," replied the usher. "Well," said the stranger, laying down the money, "if that's all, I'd like to jine in. I've had a few hours experience of this court, and no one can feel a greater contempt for it than I do, and I am willing to pay for it !" A MEAN ADVANTAGE.—" I think I've got rather the meanest husband in Detroit," exclaimed a little woman on the car the other day. Her friend asked her to ex- plain, and she continued: "I found that he was smoking fifty cents' worth of cigars per day, and I got him to agree to give me as much pin-money per week as the cigars cost. He stuck to it one week." "And then what?" "He bought him a clay pipe and a pound of ten-cent smoking tobacco, and my income is cut down to two cents a week !" ' Two KINDS Or pIISPENSE.-A murderer under sentence Of death had a number of influential friends who were exerting themselves to secure a respite from the Governor. The Sheriff believed in capital punishment, but he was a charitably-disposed man and had been doing a good deal of running around for his doomed guest. One morning he returned from such a trip and went to the prisoner. "Well," said the man eagerly, "what did the Governor say?" "My dear sir, he hasn't said anything yet; he wants time to think." "Great heavens, man! This suspense is terrible," exclaimed the criminal, dramatically. "Don't mention it," re- sponded the Sheriff, in a cheerful tone; "it ain't any- thing to what it will be if the Governor doesn't inter- fere.' How ns FOUND HER OUT.—"I have seen many strange things in my time," said Inspector B---- of the detective department, as he sat in the Bodega sipping his wine. "Brought to light no end of impostors, eh?" inquires a friend sitting by. "I believe you, my boy! But let me tell you, in strict confidence, I was myself once taken in thoroughly by a nice pretty girl. I could have vowed she was an angel." "And wasn't she?" , "Just the opposite. She had a temper like a hurricane, and when she got vexed you felt as if there was going to be an earthquake." "Good gracious but how did you find that out ?" "Well . . . you see . . . I mafried her.' WHERE THE MILK GAME ratom.—One of our bishops recently told the following story. He had gone down into the country to visit a charitable institution into which poor lads had been drafted from the East-end of London, and, in addressing them he congratulated them on the delights of their new residence. The boys looked unaccountably gloomy and downcast, and the bishop kindly asked, Are you not comfortable? Have you any complaints to make ?" At last the leader raised his hand. "The milk, my lord !" "Why, what on earth do you mean? The milk here is tenfold better than ever you had in London." "No, indeed, it ain't!" cried the boy. "In London they always buys our milk out of a nice clean shop, and here—why, here they squeezes it out of a beastly cow !" DISSIPATING ON SPONGE CAKE.—There were three Or four young Japanese students, it is said, who were in the habit of dining on Sunday at an English friend's house at Hammersmith. One of the parties was a young man of high rank and great dignity, and when, one Sun- day, he was missing from the table, the host asked with some solicitude the cause of his absence. "Oh, he can- not come," said the spokesman of the party, shaking his head sadly; "he very dissipated—very dissipated !" The host thought it best not to make any further in- quiry at the time, but after dinner, when the ladies had left the table, he ventured to ask the same young man in private, "You say, Mr. Nim Shi is not well?" "No, he not well—he very dissipated." "Bless me! He hasn't—ah—been drinking ?' "Oh, no, no I He no drink." "Not gambling, eh ?" "No, no! He no gamble." "May I ask what he has been doing, then?" "Oh, he very dissipated! He eat spongee cake alle time—lie all broke up now." UNWELCOME FIND IN A MAIL BAG.—After the mail train on this division of the Central Railroad had passed Morrow's Station one morning recently, Railway Post- master Milner unlocked the mail pouch handed on at that station. On turning back the flap of the pouch out sprang a rattlesnake ten or twelve inches long, and struck at the Postmaster. This so surprised him that it is said he jumped backward the whole length of the car, so that for a while his snakeship had complete pos- session of Uncle Sam's mail. The commotion it occa- sioned soon alarmed the passengers on the train, and by the well-directed blows of a "posse comitatus " his snakeship was soon lying a lifeless corpse. How he got there will be a case for the investigation of a special mail inspector.
